title: Trump promised to lower prices for Americans. Here's what the data shows.
summary: Just weeks before the midterm elections, 90% of Americans say prices in the U.S. are the main factor shaping their view of the economy. These charts show why.
story: President Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to lower Americans' cost of living, vowing to push gasoline prices below $2 a gallon and to deliver 2% mortgage rates. Two years later, consumers face sharply higher costs for many of the necessities he pledged to make more affordable.

Less than a month before the midterm elections, the gap between Mr. Trump's promises and the financial realities facing many Americans is fueling voter frustration over the economy. Although economic growth is solid and unemployment remains low, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a recent CBS News poll.

The financial pressures affecting Americans predate Mr. Trump's return to the White House last year. Consumers are reeling from the cumulative impact of five years of post-pandemic inflation, economists note. But his campaign promises raised hopes that he would lower consumer prices.

At the same time, some of Mr. Trump's policies have exacerbated inflation. His tariff regime contributed about 2.9 percentage points to inflation through February, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Without the tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.
Mr. Trump's decision to attack Iran in February has also led to a drawn-out conflict that has disrupted oil shipments and sharply driven up the price of oil, gas and diesel.

"It's undeniable that several of these supply shocks that the U.S. economy has been navigating through come from policy decisions made by the administration — namely, decisions to intervene in Iran and decisions to impose tariffs," Greg Daco, chief economist at investment advisory firm EY-Parthenon, told CBS News.
Inflation in September is forecast to have risen at an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August, according to economists polled by FactSet — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.
Ryan Bourne, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, said that consumers "judge the prices they're paying against the prices they paid four or five years ago, and are still shocked by it."
He added, "As a result of that, they think the economy's doing very, very badly."

The White House said that Mr. Trump's agenda "stopped Biden's inflation crisis" while creating jobs and economic growth. The administration's policies "will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News.

"The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: He signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first and sent 401(k)s to record highs," Rogers added.
The following charts show how U.S. costs have changed for expenses ranging from groceries to car insurance.
Groceries
"A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Pittsburgh on Nov. 4, 2024.
For consumers, each visit to the supermarket is a fresh reminder of inflation's impact on food costs, which have continued to rise since Mr. Trump vowed to lower grocery prices.

The cost of food prepared at home has climbed 4% since November 2024, according to Consumer Price Index data, when Mr. Trump said a vote for him would lead to lower costs. That increase comes on top of a 23% jump in food prices during the prior four years. Because consumers tend to remember what they spent on groceries before the pandemic, they get a jolt each time they visit the supermarket, said Daco of EY-Parthenon.

"Whether it's talking about gas prices or grocery prices or restaurant prices or travel prices, everybody talks about inflation," he said. "The salience of prices is what is driving this downbeat consumer morale."

Food costs are continuing to rise due to a number of factors, ranging from the elevated price of gas and diesel, which are needed to fuel farm equipment and ship items to stores, to the Trump administration's tariffs, economists said.
Gasoline

"Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon, bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares, and housing costs."  — Mr. Trump in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Sept. 5, 2024.

Gas prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. As of Oct. 9, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline was $4.37. That's up 47% from $2.98 on Feb. 27, one day before the war began, according to CBS News data. Prices at the pump are at a record high for October, according to AAA.

Diesel prices rose to a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22 and now hover around $6.28. Diesel, which is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, is a factor in consumer prices for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

Gas prices tend to have an outsized impact on consumer sentiment, influencing their views on future inflation and the broader economy, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
Energy and electricity

"By contrast, I'm announcing today that under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least half." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.

Consumers' energy bills have continued to increase this year. Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that average monthly residential electricity costs rose 12.5% between December 2024 and July of this year. Electricity bills are rising as utilities spend more to upgrade the nation's aging power grid, and overall energy demand grows amid the data center buildout.

Natural gas is also more expensive. Average monthly residential prices for natural gas rose 106% between December 2024 and July 2025, according to the EIA. Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan policy and research firm, attributes the jump to geopolitical conflict, an increase in domestic exports, extreme weather linked to climate change and rising infrastructure costs.

A July report from advocacy groups The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers found that the national average utility bill reached $280 per month in early 2026, up 12% since the end of 2024, just before Mr. Trump took office.

Many people could face even higher energy prices this winter. Americans are forecast to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes between mid-November and mid-March 2027, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, a policy organization. Homeowners who use heating oil are projected to pay an average of $2,627 over that three-month period, up roughly 50% from last year, the group said.
Car insurance

"Car insurance is up 70% to 100%, and you can't get it. … But prices will come down. You just watch, they'll come down, and they'll come down fast." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.
Car insurance costs are one area where consumers are seeing some modest relief. Data shows motorists are paying 5.5% less for vehicle coverage since premiums hit a recent high in February.

Still, insurance prices have soared in recent years along with the cost of both new and used vehicles. Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist for The Conference Board, a nonprofit that represents businesses, attributed the recent dip in premiums to increased industry competition, rather than public policy actions.
"Some of the deceleration was a result of a pushback from consumers, rather than some legislative or other action," Shulyatyeva told CBS News.
Housing and mortgage costs

"We will drive down the rates so you will be able to pay 2% again, and we will be able to finance or refinance your homes drastically at much lower costs." — Mr. Trump at a campaign rally in Tucson, Arizona, on Sept. 12, 2024.

Mortgage rates were climbing from pandemic-era lows for several years before President Trump returned to office in January of 2025. The average rate on a conventional 30-year mortgage now stands at 7.28%, up from 7.04% when Mr. Trump took office, according to Freddie Mac.
But home loan rates have been volatile, briefly dipping below 5% in February before climbing amid surging government bond yields, rising inflation and geopolitical tensions.

Borrowing costs are just one side of the struggle: Home buyers are also contending with high prices, keeping many on the sidelines as they wait for more affordable options. The median list price for a home in August was $408,333, up 4% from $392,967 since Mr. Trump took office, according to Zillow.
The gap between the income needed to afford a home, $126,487, and the U.S. median income, $86,490, is now the widest since 2005, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.
Credit card rates

"We're going to put a temporary cap on credit card interest rates. We're going to cap it around 10%. We can't let them make 25% and 30%." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Uniondale, New York, on Sept. 18, 2024.

President Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates at 10% while campaigning, an issue he also highlighted after taking office in 2025. But while the effort drew bipartisan support, the proposal fizzled.

Currently, the average credit card rate across all commercial bank accounts is 20.94%, down from 21.58% when Mr. Trump resumed office, according to Federal Reserve data. Credit experts said the rate-cap proposal would have hindered consumers' access to credit.

"Obviously, we'd love for everyone to have low rates and be free from debt. But the unintended consequence of a 10% cap would be the loss of access to credit, because banks say they wouldn't be profitable with it capped at that low rate," Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling firm, told CBS News.
Airfare
"We're going [to] … bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the New York Economic Club on Sept. 5, 2024.

Along with promising to reduce energy prices, Mr. Trump pledged to lower airfare costs for travelers. In recent months, fares have eased slightly, although CPI data shows that they remain 17% higher than in January 2025.

The war in Iran has disrupted global oil supplies and raised jet fuel costs, which are the second- biggest expense for airlines after labor costs. Facing significantly larger fuel bills, carriers are raising prices to cover the added costs.

Jet fuel now costs $4.34 a gallon, up 85% from an average of $2.35 per gallon in January 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration. Aviation analysts also point to the May shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines as another factor behind higher fares.
ACA health insurance
"I will make the ACA much, much, much better for far less money (or cost) to our greatest American citizens. …" — Mr. Trump in a Truth Social post on March 26, 2024.

Millions of Americans with an Affordable Care Act health insurance plan face sharply higher costs than a year ago. Average monthly premiums have risen to $178, or $2,136 per year, up 58% from 2025, according to a May analysis from nonprofit health group KFF.

Obamacare plan deductibles have soared from an average of $1,027 per person to $3,786, up 37% over the same period, KFF found. Prices for ACA plans spiked after Congress allowed a tax subsidy designed to lower plan costs to expire at the end of last year.
In an effort to offer relief, the Trump administration began sending $500 checks in September to nearly 1 million ACA participants in 30 states.
Prescription drugs
"When reelected as president, I will continue my efforts to protect Americans from unaffordable drug prices …" — Mr. Trump in an interview with AARP Magazine on Oct. 2, 2024.
Prescription drug prices have dropped since Mr. Trump took office in his second term, falling 3.9% after peaking in February 2025, government data show.

Mr. Trump has credited his policies lowering drug costs, with the White House stating in August that the president "has delivered" on his campaign promise. The administration cited policies such as its "most favored nation" approach, which links U.S. drug prices to those paid in other developed nations.

Experts said that while the Trump administration's policies have helped, other factors are also at play. For instance, manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are cutting their prices amid increased competition, while the nonpartisan Brookings Institution notes that more generic drugs are entering the marketplace, tempering healthcare costs.

title: AI linked to 84% of ransomware attacks, new report finds
summary: Amid escalating threats to businesses, former White House cyber chief warns autonomous attacks are already here.
story: Cybercriminals exploited artificial intelligence in ransomware attacks experienced by 84% of surveyed victims, according to a sweeping new global cybersecurity report, while 44% reported that attackers exploited their own AI systems.

The 2026 Ransomware Risk Report by cybersecurity firm Semperis polled 1,200 IT and security professionals across nine countries and eight industry sectors, revealing an evolved picture of cybercriminal enterprise—one that increasingly leverages AI to magnify its technical capabilities and escalate pressure on targets.

But the findings also underscored ransomware's human toll. According to the report, more than a third of surveyed victims faced psychological or physical threats against employees, and 14% of surveyed organizations even reported employees or family members forced to change jobs, office locations or residences as a result of sustained ransomware threats.

In all, 69% of surveyed ransomware victims experienced multiple successful attacks sometime in the previous year, with 59% of respondents paying a ransom at least once, and 87% experienced attacks targeting their identity systems, or the digital infrastructure that controls access to their networks.

For Chris Inglis, former White House National Cyber Director under former President Joe Biden, artificial intelligence represents a turning point in the capabilities ripe for cybercriminals' exploit —and he warns that a particularly consequential development is already underway: autonomous ransomware attacks.

"AI actually increases the capacity, scope, scale of attackers in understanding what perhaps might be the weaknesses in your system or perhaps increase the sophistication of their approach to you if they're trying to get you to do something you shouldn't do, that gives them an advantage, lets them in," Inglis said in an interview about the report.

The cybersecurity expert and Semperis board member previously spent three decades watching technologies mature at the National Security Agency watching as attacks required substantially less direct human involvement – no longer simply a theoretical possibility.

"AI is an inflection point in their capacities to hold the same things at risk," Inglis said. He later added, "I think we're already seeing autonomous attacks. Autonomous ransomware attacks are included in the mix."

Inglis described how a person lacking the technical expertise to penetrate an organization's networks could turn to AI to write the necessary code, effectively instructing an AI system to target a company and hold its data hostage without a sophisticated understanding of how digital infrastructure operates.

"We have democratized AI to the point where even low level models can allow that to happen," Inglis said, noting that the technology compounds the number of criminals capable of launching more technical attacks, while inviting experienced cybercriminals to penetrate networks more efficiently and on a much greater scale.
AI is changing the ransomware playbook

For years, criminals have relied on a familiar playbook: exploiting vulnerabilities, penetrating corporate networks, encrypting data and demanding a ransom payment in exchange for restored access or withholding sensitive information. Now, in more than eight out of 10 attacks, AI has been incorporated into that process.

AI has also enabled attackers to quickly identify weaknesses, tailor social engineering schemes to specific employees, automate an intrusion and readjust tactics as defenders try to react, according to Inglis.

"What's not changed is the things that people or organizations had that is of value that they would pay money or time or energy to protect," Inglis said. "And those things are still the object of a broad swath of criminals attention. They want to use whatever tools they can to try to hold those at risk so they can get you to pay them money, sometimes time, but really it's about money."
By lowering technical barriers, AI risks enabling a wider range of actors to attempt intrusions that previously demanded a wide swath of resources and more specialized training or know-how.

Tomer Bar, Semperis's associate vice president of security research, warns that AI could enable ransomware developers to produce more sophisticated malicious code, reduce development time and make investigations more challenging.
"We're starting to see more attacks with more rapid development, and attribution of these attacks will be more difficult for law enforcement," Bar says in the report.
"We'll also be less likely to see mistakes in attack encryption algorithms because attackers can test their code with [large language models.]"
When a company's own AI becomes a weapon against it

One of the report's most striking revelations is that 44% of surveyed victims experienced ransomware attacks exploiting their own AI agents or systems, a finding that raises an uncomfortable question for businesses and government agencies racing to integrate the technology into its networks.

Courtney Guss, Semperis's associate vice president of crisis management, warns that autonomous AI agents can create security risks when they seek additional permissions or interact with sensitive corporate systems.

"If your company is adopting AI agents, you should consider that at some point, those agents will try to compromise your identity systems — even if that action isn't meant to be malicious," Guss writes in the report.

"That's just how they operate. AI agents typically try to accomplish their assigned tasks by any means they can." Guss continued. "One way they can gain more ability to operate in the environment is by getting permissions to other systems. The fastest path to get those permissions is to compromise your identity system, which effectively puts the agent into 'god mode,' enabling it to grant itself whichever permissions it needs to accomplish its task. Unfortunately, the agent then becomes a ticking time bomb."
Unlike conventional software operating, some AI agents possess the ability to use multiple applications at once and make educated decisions on behalf of their users.
If an attacker manipulates just one of those agents—or compromises the credentials and permissions it relies upon—the attacker gains another way of moving deeper into an organization's systems.
Still, Inglis cautions against assumptions that AI necessarily makes an organization more vulnerable to outside intruders.

"Many attackers already do what's called living off the land – they'll move into your digital infrastructure, onto your property or digital property, and they'll use the tools that you have there or the insights or the data set," Inglis said. "To blend in, to navigate the landscape, they try not to stand out, and they do that by using your tools. If AI is one of your tools, they'll use those, but the weakness that let them in is probably the same weakness that existed before."

Inglis argues that the fundamental vulnerability often lies within a company's failure to control access to its networks or digital infrastructure in the first place. Rather than abandon AI out of fear, Inglis argues that organizations must embrace its defensive potential.
"I would turn that around. Flip the script," he said. "You must use AI in order to counter that threat, and you must use AI for affirmative purposes."
Julia Kimani-Burnham contributed to this report.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:00 a.m. on Oct. 14, 2026.

title: Trump pardons 2 auto workers on stage during rally in Alaska
summary: President Trump granted onstage pardons to two Alaska auto shop owners who pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act during a rally Tuesday — an unusually public use of the president's clemency power.
story: President Trump during a political rally in the state late Tuesday granted onstage pardons to two Alaska auto shop owners who pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act — an unusually public use of the president's clemency power.

The president said the two men — Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming — were "wrongly charged," and cast the charges against the two men as an example of how the Biden-era Justice Department "viciously targeted the Alaskan way of life."

Czubak, Fleming and a third man named Michael Hanzuk owned an auto shop that specialized in diesel vehicles called Arm Rippin Toys, according to court records. Federal prosecutors say they offered to remove the emission control systems in customers' vehicles for a fee of $1,140 to $5,445, in part by modifying their physical components and preventing their diagnostics systems from noticing a problem, causing the vehicles to spew more pollutants.
All three men pleaded guilty to conspiracy to violate the Clean Air Act in 2022. They were each sentenced to five years of probation, $66,000 in fines and community service.
During Tuesday's pre-midterm election rally in Wasilla, Mr. Trump called Czubak and Fleming onto the stage and said to an aide: "Bring me the pardons!"

"Think of it: They want to put them in jail for 10 years because they fixed an engine. How sick?" the president said. "Now if you murder somebody, no problem. Unless a Republican does the murdering. Then it's, you know, the electric chair, right?"
Mr. Trump signed the pardons at the podium and handed them to Czubak and Fleming, drawing cheers from rallygoers as the president held one of the pardons up to the crowd.
The president said he was also "taking care of" a third person. He did not name the other person, but the third co-owner of Arm Rippin Toys, Hanzuk, received a pardon last month.

"When you give somebody a pardon, they say that means, and I don't know how this works and why it's an expression, but it's well-used, that means you're as clean as a newborn baby's ass," the president said. "I never understood that. Why is that so clean?"
Czubak and Fleming briefly addressed the crowd, with Fleming saying the charges against the three "really did destroy us."
"We're not criminals. We're not trying to hurt anybody," he said. "We want to help Alaskans. We want to help people with diesel trucks, with vehicles, across the world."
CBS News has reached out to Czubak, Fleming and Hanzuk's attorneys for comment.

Earlier this year, Mr. Trump granted a pardon to Mac Spurlock, another diesel mechanic who was also charged with violating the Clean Air Act by removing pollution control systems — a case that the president mentioned during Tuesday's rally.

Spurlock and his supporters, including GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska, argue the engine modifications that he performed were necessary to prevent emissions systems from malfunctioning due to Alaska's frigid weather.

Sullivan applauded Spurlock's pardon in July, calling the charges the work of "overzealous federal prosecutors" and arguing the Environmental Protection Agency's rules should be modified to account for cold-weather states. Tuesday's rally was held in part to help Sullivan fend off a challenge from Democratic candidate Mary Peltola.
The Justice Department announced in January it would "no longer pursue criminal charges under the Clean Air Act based on allegations of tampering with onboard diagnostic devices."

During the Biden administration, officials took a different tack, warning in a statement on the Arm Rippin Toys charges that cutting out emissions controls "results in a massive increase in air pollution from even a single vehicle." Scot Adair, former special agent in charge of the EPA's Criminal Investigation Division in Alaska vowed to "hold accountable those who jeopardize human health and the environment for the sake of profit."

Mr. Trump and members of his administration have railed against other environmental regulations, relaxing fuel economy standards and ending an EPA policy that gave credits to car manufacturers that installed start-stop emissions systems.
The president has also frequently used his pardon power to grant clemency to political allies and people who — like him — argue they were wrongly prosecuted.

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle ousted as ambassador over corruption allegations
summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle said she is stepping aside as U.S. ambassador to Greece, days after reports that she offered access to officials in exchange for help paying off her debt.
story: Washington — Kimberly Guilfoyle said Tuesday she would step aside as U.S. ambassador to Greece after the White House asked her to resign, days after reports that she offered access to administration officials in exchange for help paying off her debt.

"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said during her first press briefing Tuesday, breaking the news. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."
The president, who said he hasn't spoken with Guilfoyle, soon confirmed she is leaving her post.
"She will not be there. I didn't like what I read," he told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on his way to campaign in Alaska.

The move came days after an associate shared text messages indicating she had asked him for $100,000 to pay her American Express bill before her Senate confirmation hearing last year. The Wall Street Journal first reported the messages last week.
In recent days, Guilfoyle had expressed reluctance to step down, but the White House briefing on Tuesday left her with little choice, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
Guilfoyle confirmed her plans to resign in a post on X less than two hours after Zacharia's comments.
"While my time as ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," she wrote.
But she also denied the allegations against her and said she intends to "rigorously defend" her name.

"Serving as the United States Ambassador to Greece has been the honor of a lifetime," she wrote. "I will forever be grateful to President Donald J. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for entrusting me with the extraordinary privilege of representing the greatest country in the history of the world."
There were no names circulating Tuesday in the White House for a new ambassador to Greece.
Guilfoyle has few remaining allies in the Trump administration. Her former fiancé, Donald Trump Jr., has been polite to her but no longer has much contact with her, sources said.
The move to oust Guilfoyle comes after the president told reporters Monday he was "looking at" firing her, explaining he was "not happy."

Businessman Eric Deters said in an interview with CBS News last week that Guilfoyle asked him in July 2025 to wire $100,000 to her American Express account so her credit card debt wouldn't show up on her financial disclosures as she awaited Senate confirmation.

Deters characterized her request as "pay to play," and said he had sought help from Guilfoyle with access to Trump administration officials, including the attorney general and IRS commissioner. White House officials were told that the text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters were authentic, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News last week.

Deters told CBS News that "at that moment in time, I didn't have $100,000 to spare to give to Kimberly Guilfoyle, or I actually would have been a dumbass enough to do it." He said he made up an "excuse" that his wife wouldn't go along with it.
Guilfoyle appeared at her confirmation hearing in mid-July 2025 and was confirmed that September.

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle had boasted in January about Greek tycoons who were footing the bill for her luxury travel and expressed outrage about being blocked from a dinner for Eric Trump during the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.

title: Trump officials now leaning against execution livestream, sources say
summary: Last week, the Pentagon had said the execution of the ex-Army major convicted of killing 13 in 2009 would be livestreamed.
story: Trump administration officials are leaning against livestreaming the execution of the ex-Army major convicted of the killing of 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, sources familiar with the discussions said. Last week, the Pentagon had said that the public would be able to view the execution live.
President Trump had not yet made a final decision on Tuesday, two of the sources told CBS News.
White House and Pentagon spokespeople didn't immediately comment.
There has been pressure from Congress and elsewhere not to livestream Nidal Hasan's execution by firing squad, which is scheduled to take place on Dec. 3.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said last Thursday in an interview with Real America's Voice that the Pentagon planned to make the execution public.

"He's going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be," Hegseth said. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."

CNN reported earlier Tuesday that Mr. Trump and his advisers were debating whether to air the firing squad execution live, and that Mr. Trump had remarked privately that he didn't initially know Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down.
Several top Republicans in recent days expressed opposition to livestreaming Hasan's execution, and Vice President JD Vance said that if it were broadcast live, "I'm not going to be watching it."
As the president departed for a campaign rally in Alaska on Tuesday, a reporter asked him whether he's decided to allow the execution to be livestreamed. "We're looking at it," Mr. Trump replied.

GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson also acknowledged colleagues "who have concerns" in an interview with CBS News national correspondent and chief Washington analyst Robert Costa. Among them, he added, is "the concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists." Johnson also said he would not watch the execution, and he told Costa, "I need to tell the White House what some of my colleagues think about that, and not everybody is in favor of the idea."
This story published first on CBS News at 6:36 p.m. on Oct. 13, 2026.

title: OpenAI employee accused of planting recording device in office
summary: A Saudi national who worked at OpenAI as an engineer is suspected of planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms.
story: An OpenAI employee suspected of secretly planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms has been arrested on criminal charges, the Justice Department said Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and made his initial appearance in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on Tuesday. Alfozan was charged with trying to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
Prosecutors said that Alfozan had worked at OpenAI as an engineer since July 2025.

On Sept. 30, the company's employees discovered the audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television inside an executive conference room. The company later determined that the recording device had been concealed in toilet paper and installed about two days before it was discovered.

The meeting room where it was hidden was often used by OpenAI's employees to discuss highly confidential and proprietary matters, including research, product plans and business development, the Justice Department said.
In a statement, OpenAI said that after discovering the device, it contacted the FBI and has terminated the employee accused of planting it.

"The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work. At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company said.

"We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a post on X that the FBI and its partners had carried out the arrest and that the investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan's attorney, William Pernik, noted to CBS News that his client is presumed innocent, and cautioned against "jumping to conclusions at this very early stage of the case when very little information is known," or seeking to "politicize" a prosecution based on factors like nationality.

The criminal complaint, made public on Tuesday, alleged that Alfozan used a productivity tool to make inquiries about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, and locations of "leadership and exec" and external partner meetings.

Other evidence gathered in the investigation, meanwhile, showed that a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse had also submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30, related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating and remote accessing a continuous audio recording device.
A photograph included in the complaint also shows that Alfozan entered the conference room where the device was hidden on Oct. 5 and looked behind the television.

That same day, the complaint says Alfozan left his bag unattended in another room, and the company's security personnel opened it and found his ID, wallet and another recording device similar to the one planted in the conference room.
Alfozan is due to appear in federal court again on Oct. 19 for a detention hearing.

title: Judge blocks Trump admin. from felling trees at D.C. golf course
summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes blocked the Trump administration from cutting down trees at East Potomac Golf Links through Oct. 26.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Tuesday barred the Trump administration from removing trees at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C., for another two weeks after hundreds of trees were felled at the historic public course over the weekend.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said in a brief order that the Department of the Interior and National Park Service may not cut down any further trees at East Potomac through Oct. 26. She also said that through that date, the Trump administration must provide the court and plaintiffs, the D.C. Preservation League and two local golfers, with three business days' notice before "making any irreparable modification to any permanent form or feature" of the course.
Reyes said the D.C. Preservation League and golfers will likely be harmed without relief. The plaintiffs are challenging President Trump's planned overhaul of East Potomac.

"The administration has time and again tried to avoid the law in their mad rush toward converting a public recreation space to a high-end golf course and today's order will stop them from doing further irreparable harm to a precious public resource," lawyers for the D.C. Preservation League and two residents said. "We are pleased that the court intervened and will prevent additional work while we seek more lasting relief."

The brief order comes after the judge fiercely chastised the Justice Department during a nearly four-hour-long hearing Monday. She called the hearing after learning Friday afternoon that the National Park Service planned to remove an estimated 529 trees at East Potomac golf course as part of a "tree management and cultural landscape rehabilitation project."

The D.C. Preservation League then told the court in a filing Sunday that the crew had cut down all 529 trees on Saturday alone, including "healthy, mature oaks and maples," and had planned to remove "hundreds" more "imminently," but rain impacted the work.
A Justice Department lawyer, Marissa Piropato, told Reyes that 430 trees in total were felled. Another roughly 99 have been identified for removal, she said.

For months, Reyes had reiterated to the government that it must provide advance notice to the plaintiffs and the court of plans to conduct any construction or similar activity at East Potomac, allowing her the opportunity to review that action and, if warranted, issue an order.
But the Justice Department did not submit a filing about the planned tree removals until just before 5 p.m. Friday.
"You did not do your best. You did your absolute worst," Reyes told Piropato of the Justice Department's efforts to notify the court and plaintiffs of the planned tree removals.
The judge told Piropato and other government lawyers that they "lost credibility."

She ordered Kevin Griess, superintendent of the National Mall and Memorial Parks, and Frank Lands, deputy director of operations for the National Park Service, to testify about what led to the felling of the 430 trees at the course and who gave the go-ahead for the removals to take place Saturday.
Reyes scheduled another hearing for Oct. 19 and ordered Jessica Bowron, acting director of the National Park Service, and Gregory Wischer, deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, to appear.

title: Bipartisan senators call Russia diesel deal a "betrayal" of Ukraine
summary: A bipartisan group of senators urged President Trump to withdraw from his diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and rescind a move to waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector.
story: Washington — A bipartisan group of senators on Tuesday urged President Trump to withdraw from his diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and rescind a move to waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector, saying it "damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine."
"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the senators wrote.

Mr. Trump announced last week that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to have Moscow immediately release 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by millions more in the coming months. Putin said Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the American and global markets." And the Treasury Department also announced that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."

The move, which comes as Americans are struggling with high gas and diesel prices amid the war with Iran, has sparked scrutiny from both sides of the aisle. In their letter on Tuesday, a dozen senators criticized the effort, including six Republicans: Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky and John Cornyn of Texas.

Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Dick Durbin of Illinois, Sheldon Whitehouse and Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Chris Coons of Delaware also signed on to the letter.

The senators wrote that although Americans support ending the Russia-Ukraine war, a brokered peace "must be on just terms," and uphold "democratic values, the sovereignty and security of Ukraine, and their people's right to choose their future."
The deal struck with Putin, the senators wrote, "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans."

The senators acknowledged the "urgent need" to lower energy costs for Americans. But they said allowing Russian diesel to be sold on global markets "will offer limited to no relief to Americans" and would have a "negligible impact on fuel prices," while the revenues the Kremlin would receive would "undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea."

Congress approved a Russian sanctions package just last month, which Mr. Trump signed into law. The senators noted that the law granted the president "authorities to broker a just and fair peace," arguing that those authorities "require you to apply economic pressure on Russia" and "thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict."

"For decades, America has stood as the bastion of freedom against tyranny, and American presidents have embodied our nation's resistance to tyrants," they wrote, urging the president to withdraw from the agreement, rescind the Treasury Department's move to waive sanctions, and execute the authorities under the Russia sanctions legislation. "Maintain our legacy — and the duty America holds — as leader of the free world."

title: Supreme Court takes up dispute over access to DOGE records
summary: The Supreme Court agreed to take up a dispute involving a government watchdog group's attempt to get information from the Department of Government Efficiency​.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to take up a dispute involving a government watchdog group's attempt to get information from the Department of Government Efficiency as part of a fight over whether the controversial cost-cutting entity is subject to public records law.

Arguments in the case, U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, will likely take place in early 2027, with a decision coming by that summer. The Trump administration has attempted to prevent the group, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, from getting information about DOGE, which spearheaded government-wide firings of federal workers and cancellations of government contracts.
The case arose out of a Freedom of Information Act request CREW filed in early 2025 for information about DOGE, including its organizational chart and financial disclosures.

But the Trump administration declined to process the request, arguing that DOGE is not subject to FOIA because it is housed within the Executive Office of the President and is a purely advisory entity. As a result, CREW sued and sought a court order declaring that DOGE is covered by FOIA and requiring the task force to respond to the records request.

A judge went on to allow the group to collect limited information about DOGE's structure and the scope of its authority, and to conduct a deposition with its administrator, Amy Gleason, to better address the question of whether it is an advisory panel that falls outside FOIA's scope or is an agency subject to the law.
The Trump administration attempted to stop the discovery process, and as part of that effort, went on to file an emergency appeal with the Supreme Court.

In a 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court set aside the lower court order that required DOGE to turn over information about its work. The high court took issue with some of the material DOGE had to provide to CREW, which "require[s] the Government to disclose the content of intra-Executive Branch USDS recommendations and whether those recommendations were followed."
"Separation of powers concerns counsel judicial deference and restraint in the context of discovery regarding internal executive branch communications," the Supreme Court said.

The high court sent the case back to the lower courts for more proceedings and ordered the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to take "appropriate action to narrow" the district court's discovery order.

When the case returned to the lower courts, CREW withdrew its request for some categories of records and sought only information on DOGE's structure, its directives to cancel federal contracts and fire government workers, and examples of DOGE exercising substantial independent authority, like by gaining access to sensitive systems.
The D.C. Circuit then allowed that information-gathering to proceed, finding that CREW had narrowed its request for information in a way that was consistent with the Supreme Court's order.

The Trump administration appealed to the high court, arguing that if allowed, CREW would receive much of the information it sought in its FOIA requests before a court has said whether DOGE is even covered by the law.

"The decision below intrudes into the autonomy and confidentiality of presidential advisors and augurs time-consuming and burdensome discovery litigation, including through a deposition of USDS Administrator Amy Gleason," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in a filing. "Beyond this case, the court of appeals' FOIA ruling threatens to burden future presidential administrations with FOIA suits designed to leverage discovery against advisors in the Executive Office."

President Trump announced DOGE's creation soon after he began his second term as part of his plans to slash the size of the federal government. Led by billionaire Elon Musk and housed within the Executive Office of the President, the task force deployed team members to agencies across the executive branch. DOGE was behind efforts to shrink the federal workforce and cut contracts worth billions of dollars, as well as to shutter agencies like the U.S. Institute of Peace and U.S. Agency for International Development.
But the agency sparked concerns with its attempts to gain access to sensitive databases kept by the Internal Revenue Service, Social Security Administration and Office of Personnel Management.
Musk, who was working as a "special government employee," left DOGE in May 2025.

While DOGE's goal was to decrease government spending, an analysis from the Government Accountability Office found that the Trump administration spent $9.5 billion on employee administrative leave costs in 2025, a sixfold increase from 2023. The GAO said $6.7 billion of that total was because of employees who accepted a buyout offer from the Trump administration that was part of DOGE's initiative to shrink the federal government.

title: Talarico was home in Texas during campaign absence, photos indicate
summary: James Talarico's campaign shared security camera footage with CBS News that appears to show him at his home in Texas for the first eight days of this month — pushing back on claims that Talarico was hiding the reasons for his disappearance.
story: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's campaign shared security camera footage with CBS News that appears to show Talarico at his home in Texas for the first eight days of this month — pushing back on claims that Talarico was hiding the reasons for his disappearance.
Talarico was absent from the campaign trail for almost two weeks, saying he caught a bad case of the flu. The disappearance drew criticism and speculation from his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.

But on Monday, Talarico's campaign shared a set of security camera images that they say show the state lawmaker and Democratic candidate at his home in Texas every day from Oct. 1 to Oct. 8, one day before Talarico made a public appearance.

The eight timestamped images — which include watermarks from home security camera company SimpliSafe — appeared to have been taken from a camera in the backyard of Talarico's house in the state capital of Austin. CBS News matched features in the backyard to recent satellite imagery of Talarico's address. Though low resolution, the photos show a male figure with brown hair at various times of day and wearing different outfits.
The images were first reported by The New York Times.
The mental health facility at the center of the conspiracy theories, Lindner Center of Hope in Mason, Ohio, also wrote on social media that Talarico "has never received treatment" there.
Talarico campaign spokesman J.T. Ennis said in a statement that claims Talarico was elsewhere were "a lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory."
"Last week James Talarico was home in Austin, Texas recovering from the flu," Ennis said.
Timeline: What we know about James Talarico's whereabouts
Talarico was not seen in public for just under two weeks, from late September to late Friday.

His last known in-person event in Texas took place on Saturday, Sept. 26, in the Dallas suburb of Carrollton. Two days later, he was in New York City for a series of fundraisers, including a joint fundraiser with Ohio Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown hosted by Robert De Niro.
On Sept. 30, Talarico pulled out of an in-person conversation with Javier Palomarez, president of the United States Hispanic Business Council. He instead appeared for a virtual Q&A.

"I was starting to feel under the weather a few days ago," Talarico told the audience, apologizing for not appearing in person. "And last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas and I was diagnosed with the flu. So I'm running a fever and I'm at my most contagious right now." (He later told a reporter he went to his primary care physician.)

A day later, on Oct. 1, Talarico's campaign called to cancel an appearance at the Central Texas African American Civic Engagement Symposium scheduled for the upcoming week, according to Essien Ita, the group's leader. Ita told CBS News that Talarico's staff declined to reschedule the appearance, and said they had canceled other events through Oct. 5.
The following week, President Trump traveled to San Antonio to campaign with Paxton. The president and Paxton, the state attorney general, both referenced Talarico's absence.

"I hear the guy has disappeared – nobody knows. You know where he is? He's sick because he's forced to eat meat for political reasons and he's throwing up all over the place," Mr. Trump said, referencing Talarico's past comments on trying to reduce meat consumption. (Talarico has denied that he is a vegan.)

Earlier in the rally, Paxton said: "When I came in here today, we were on day 11 of James Talarico not showing up in public and canceling all public appearances. Where do you think they hid that little socialist?" He then had the audience yell "Where Is James Talarico?" in unison.
Talarico was seen in public for the first time this month on Friday, Oct. 9, when a campaign spokesperson posted a video of him greeting festivalgoers at the Austin City Limits Music Festival.
On the same day, Talarico told CBS News in a text: "Feeling much better. Back on the trail!"

Talarico had several other public appearances over the weekend, attending a Kasey Musgraves concert in San Antonio on Saturday and giving interviews on Sunday to NBC's Dallas-Fort Worth station and The Dallas Morning News' editorial board.

"It wasn't anything worse than a nasty case of the flu. And so I was in bed and, you know, drinking lots of liquids. Unfortunately, the campaign made me work from home, so I didn't even get full days off," he told a local NBC reporter, saying he didn't want to get anyone else sick.
Paxton suggested something was amiss, saying Talarico "owes Texans answers."
"James Talarico claims he was missing for 13 days because he had the flu," Paxton wrote in a post on X over the weekend. "Who actually believes that?"
At around the same time, social media users began speculating — without evidence — that Talarico had flown to Ohio for mental health treatment.

Then, on Sunday, conservative social media personalities shared an unverified recording in which somebody appeared to call Ohio's Lindner Center of Hope to ask whether Talarico was checked in. A staff member at the mental health center ostensibly said he had been discharged.
CBS News could neither authenticate nor debunk the veracity of the call. The Lindner Center of Hope said publicly that Talarico did not receive treatment at the mental health facility.
The local NBC station asked Talarico about the rumors. He denied them and said: "It's a good reminder that you can't believe everything you read on the internet."

title: Rep. Omar's D.C. home searched by DHS investigators
summary: Sources say the investigation centers on Rep. Ilhan Omar's immigration documents, involving paperwork filled out by her late father when she was a child.
story: Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home was the target of a raid early Monday morning by ICE's investigations unit.
Sources say the investigation centers on Omar's immigration paperwork. The documents in question date back to Omar's childhood, involving paperwork completed by her late father when she was a child.

Omar's office said in a statement that Omar had "done nothing wrong" and called the raid an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."
Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, posted Monday on social media, "I'm ok," adding "I will not be silenced."

"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar wrote. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation."
Homeland Security Investigations, or HSI, the department's criminal investigative arm, is leading the investigation, with the Department of Justice assisting.
Investigators are examining potential allegations of false statements and immigration fraud, according to sources familiar with the investigation.
Attorney General Todd Blanche was personally aware of the search, with the Justice Department consulting its Public Integrity section, sources said.

HSI has jurisdiction over federal offenses including immigration document fraud, identity fraud and immigration benefit fraud. Unlike ICE's deportation-focused operations, HSI special agents conduct criminal investigations and execute federal search warrants.
In a statement, the Justice Department confirmed that the HSI executed a search warrant secured by the DOJ. The statement said it was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation."

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, whip Rep. Katherine Clark and caucus chair Rep. Pete Aguilar called the raid on Omar's home "deeply disturbing" and said it "raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump's adversaries."
Omar is a frequent target of President Trump. The president told reporters he "had nothing to do with" Monday's raid.
"I think she's a terrible person, but that's really up to the DOJ," he said.
Border czar Tom Homan said in September that there was an "ongoing criminal investigation" into the congresswoman.
"I'm confirming that ICE is, yeah — look, I said months ago that there's something that's been reported and needs to be looked at," Homan told Fox News in September.
Omar said at the time that she had not been contacted in connection to any investigation.

title: Data center boom puts GOP in a bind before midterms
summary: Cleanview Research found 75% of data centers being built and 80% of data centers in the planning stage are in predominantly GOP states, as public opposition to data centers grows.
story: A year ago, there weren't many voters talking about data centers. Now, the massive facilities being built to satisfy the enormous computing needs of the AI boom have become one of the most explosive issues of the 2026 midterms, and their construction is opening a divide between the Trump administration and Republicans running in state and federal races this fall.

When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, most data centers were being built in blue states. But by 2025, 68% of data centers online were in red states. Now, 75% of data centers under construction and 80% of data centers in the planning stage are in predominantly Republican states, according to new data from Cleanview Research, an independent energy market intelligence company tracking data center development.

"Red states have more of a history of accepting large, energy intensive, infrastructure projects — even those that might have detrimental effects on communities," said Chris Millay, a data center analyst at the macroeconomic consultancy Greenmantle. He also points to the relative lack of environmental regulation and the availability of open land as reasons rural states are receiving more investment.

President Trump sees the AI race as critical to the economy and national security, and he's one of data centers' biggest boosters. At a recent Ohio rally, he said of data centers, "We want them … look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio — you can't just turn them off. They'll go to China."

He has repeatedly dismissed public opposition to data centers, posting on Truth Social that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." Mr. Trump has also resisted regulation, though he has called on developers to give back to local communities through education, lower taxes, job creation and energy cost protections.

Red states may be hosting most of the boom, and increasingly, communities living next to data centers are pushing back. People who live near data centers have reported concerns about their property values, noise, higher energy bills and resource depletion. Meanwhile, calls for moratoriums are spreading through communities across the country.
Overall, opposition to data centers outweighs support by 30 points, with polls showing the majority of Republicans oppose the construction of data centers near them.

"It's such a consensus issue it's really impossible to take the other side," said Millay. "When voters see a politician who supports data centers, they think, 'Well, how am I going to trust him with my job?'"

Some of the president's closest allies have begun to break with him on the issue. In Texas, which has the most data centers under construction, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott has paused environmental permits and grid connections for new data centers. Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, is in a surprisingly close race against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

In Texas' tight Senate race, the Republican nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, wants to end Texas' sales tax break for data centers. He has also said they should be held criminally liable if they power AI chatbots that endanger children.
Data centers seem to be the single issue where Democratic and Republican candidates sound nearly identical.
In Ohio, Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, said in a press release, "I am calling on our Statehouse to pass a conditional moratorium on data centers."

Her GOP opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, has gone further. He vowed to "issue an executive order on my first day in office to immediately halt the approval of any new data center project announcements in Ohio," and to keep that pause in place until lawmakers pass his "Ohioans-First" law, which would require data centers to provide free electricity to surrounding residents.
A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that data centers are a weak point for Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, with voters favoring his opponent by an 11-point margin on the issue.
Campaigns have spent $45 million this year on ads that mention data centers — most of them in opposition — according to AdImpact.

In Georgia, where candidates have spent nearly $13 million on ads mentioning data centers — more than any other state — the Republican gubernatorial candidate, Rick Jackson, is sticking with Mr. Trump. While the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, is calling for a temporary moratorium on construction, Jackson says the decision should be left up to local officials.

Jackson made the case for data centers at a recent press conference, saying he wanted "to educate people on the benefit if they want [a data center]." Some counties, he said, expect they "will have zero property taxes after the data center goes in." Effingham County, where OpenAI plans a $20 billion data center, has pledged to use some of that revenue to cut homeowners' property taxes.

Because most of the next wave of data centers is largely planned in states Mr. Trump won in 2024, the choices Republican candidates make, siding with voters or with the president, could decide whether those projects are paused, made more expensive or even canceled.

title: Trump says he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle
summary: "Well, we're looking at it," President Trump said when asked if he's considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.
story: Washington — President Trump said he and his administration are "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle from her position as U.S. ambassador to Greece, after an associate of Guilfoyle's alleged she asked him to wire $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing.
"Well, we're looking at it," the president told reporters on his way to Ohio when asked if he's considering firing Guilfoyle. "We're not happy."

Guilfoyle is aware that Mr. Trump is debating firing her, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. She has been talking to her lawyer and asking Trump administration aides for advice, the sources said.

Businessman Eric Deters told CBS News last week he has "no doubt it was pay-to-play" when Guilfoyle asked for funds. Deters also provided CBS News with screenshots of his texts with Guilfoyle, including one message in which she appeared to ask him to wire money. Deters said he never gave her the money.
"Unfortunately for Kimberly Guilfoyle, at that time, at that moment in time, I didn't have $100,000 to spare to give to Kimberly Guilfoyle, or I actually would have been a dumbass enough to do it."

White House officials were told that the text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters were authentic, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News last week. Some Trump aides expressed displeasure about Guilfoyle's actions, they said.
Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of the texts to The Wall Street Journal, which was first to report on them.

The Journal also reported this weekend that Guilfoyle boasted in audio recordings about Greek businessmen who paid for her travel, and reportedly encouraged foreign governments to do business with one of the tycoons.

Guilfoyle, nominated by Mr. Trump to serve as his top envoy to Greece, is the ex-fiancée of Donald Trump Jr. Her confirmation hearing was held in July 2025, and she was confirmed in September of that year.

She was highly visible during Secretary of State Marco Rubio's visit to Greece last week. At the time, Rubio did not respond to questions about Deter's allegations, telling reporters: "I'm not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago."

title: Zelenskyy says Russia isn't honoring Trump's energy ceasefire
summary: Within a day of President Trump announcing an "energy ceasefire," Ukraine said Russia had struck a power plant and other energy facilities across the country.
story: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that so far, "there is no indication that Russia is complying" with an energy ceasefire announced by President Trump the day before.
Just hours after Mr. Trump's announcement, Zelenskyy said Russia struck a power plant in eastern Ukraine. By Monday afternoon, Russia had attacked six additional energy facilities across Ukraine.

"Ukraine is ready to guarantee the energy ceasefire, as announced by the American President, and Russia must take corresponding steps," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "As of now, there is no indication that Russia is complying with the conditions outlined by the American President."

Asked Monday about reports that Russia had violated the energy ceasefire, Mr. Trump said: "I'm not sure about that, and we'll take a look. But all I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war." He also said "there's been violations on both sides."
The U.S. president later told reporters that he believes Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy."
Over the last year, Mr. Trump has made several attempts at brokering deals to halt strikes on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine that failed to materialize or were quickly violated.

In January, Mr. Trump claimed that Putin agreed not to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure for a week, but Russia attacked Kyiv's power and heating plants four days later. In September, Mr. Trump said both Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to refrain from striking one another's energy infrastructure, but neither side halted attacks.
Zelenskyy told CBS News in an interview after the September proposal that Ukraine would be willing to agree to such a moratorium but doubted Russia would ever reciprocate.

One reason for the Kremlin's intransigence is that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have a relatively greater impact than Ukraine's. Ukrainian strikes primarily target Russian oil and gas infrastructure, attempting to cut into the energy revenues Russia uses to fund its war effort.

The attacks have brought Russian oil refining to a 20-year low and reduced diesel production by 30% in 2026, according to the International Energy Agency, but Russia's economy has shown little sign of collapse.

"For Russia, Ukraine's attacks are an inconvenience and an inflationary pressure," Alexander Kolyandr, director for Europe at Eurasia Group, told CBS News. "It is definitely damaging Russia's economy, but it isn't putting it on the verge of collapse."

Russia — with more drones and missiles and an economy 10 times the size of Ukraine's — is able to inflict more relative pain on both the country's economy and its civilians. Ukraine has already begun to experience power outages this fall as Russia hammers its power grid heading into winter.

"Because the Ukrainian economy is so much smaller than the Russian one, the relative effect is much higher," Kolyandr said. "And the Russians by and large do not distinguish between civilian and military infrastructure. Their theory is that any kind of infrastructure is used or can be used for military purposes."

Last winter, as Ukrainians faced frequent power and heating outages through one of the coldest winters in recent memory, Mr. Trump requested Putin stop striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. This week, though, he has directed pressure toward Ukraine.

The pressure comes as Mr. Trump grapples with high global energy prices — a situation he has argued has more to do with the Russia-Ukraine war than the Iran war. Last week, Mr. Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to sell some diesel to the U.S. and global markets, a change of course after years of U.S. efforts to block Russia from financing its war effort by selling petroleum products abroad.

A European official and a Ukrainian official told CBS News that the Trump administration has threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine does not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.

The Ukrainian official said that Ukraine's government is taking the threats very seriously as intelligence sharing allows Ukraine to know where and when Russia launches its ballistic missiles from, and the PURL program is the only way Ukraine can purchase its Patriot air defense missiles, already in short supply.
The Financial Times was first to report the American threats to pause intelligence and weapons shipments to Ukraine.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.
Zelenskyy said progress toward an energy ceasefire hinges on the White House's willingness to impose more pressure on Russia.
"A lot depends on America's position for de-escalation to actually succeed," he wrote on X. "Pressure on Russia is needed."

title: Republicans voice concerns over livestream execution plan
summary: President Trump said he approved of livestreaming the execution, but suggested the decision may not be final.
story: Washington — A growing number of Republicans are voicing concern over the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood shooter in December — or at the very least, saying they won't be watching.

Over the weekend, President Trump said the administration was still making a determination about whether the firing-squad execution would be livestreamed, after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that it would be. The execution of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, is scheduled for Dec. 3.
House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News that some in the House Republican conference don't approve, and said he planned on bringing those concerns to the White House.

"There are colleagues who have concerns," Johnson told national correspondent and chief Washington analyst Robert Costa in an interview. "The concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists. You know, we've got to think through the policy implications of all that. I wouldn't be watching it if it was aired. But there's a lot of opinions on that. I think there's still some time to talk about that. ... I need to tell the White House what some of my colleagues think about that, and not everybody is in favor of the idea."
Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said there is "no need to livestream any execution, including this one," urging the Pentagon to change course.

"I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," she wrote on X. "It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks. How we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself, so I urge the Pentagon to reverse this gruesome decision."

Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said in a statement, "The death penalty is not entertainment." He said families of the victims deserve justice. "But publicizing the execution of religious extremists provides exactly what terrorists crave: an audience. It converts the most consequential punishment a government can impose into a public spectacle."
"Justice will be served, but the United States of America does not and should not livestream executions," Republican Rep. Ann Wagner of Missouri wrote on X.

Rep. Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania wrote, "An execution shouldn't be a live-streamed spectacle. The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show."
Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina on Friday called livestreaming the execution "beyond disgusting."

Only one Republican member of Congress has publicly voiced clear support for livestreaming the execution — Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee.: "Excellent. Public execution is what this terrorist deserves," he wrote on X. "We will be watching."
Vice President JD Vance said Friday that he wouldn't be watching if it's livestreamed, and added, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the livestreaming decision on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" this weekend. Asked if the administration risks making Hasan a martyr, Mullin responded, "No one has to watch it." Pressed further on whether the decision risks radicalizing others, Mullin said, "I think people need to understand if you attack— if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the— that the punishment fits the crime."
On Saturday, Mr. Trump floated the possibility that the plans could still change.

"There are two thoughts: don't show it and show it," the president told reporters at the White House Saturday. "'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I'll make a decision."
The president has given seemingly conflicting information as to whether he was involved in the decision to livestream the execution.

When a reporter asked the president Friday if he authorized or approved the livestreaming decision, he said, "Absolutely, I did." But in an interview with CNY Central Syracuse later that day, he said he "wasn't involved in that decision" to livestream the execution, while saying he understood that decision was made to "have it serve as an example."
