title: How Iran made the Houthis into such a problem
summary: 10 years ago, few people had heard of the Houthis. Here's how the Yemeni rebels have become Iran's "most powerful proxy."
story: Yemen's Houthi rebels have morphed over the last decade from being a little-known group in northwest Yemen, to Iran's most potent ally in the region and a central opponent of the United States and its allies across the Middle East.

While Iran's other proxy forces have been depleted in recent years, the Houthis have taken center stage in the Middle East, offering yet another example of how a smaller, guerrilla-style force that's dug in on the ground can cause asymmetric damage through hard-to-repel aerial attacks.

In support of their Iranian benefactors, the Houthis launched initial attacks on Israel not long after the U.S. joined the Jewish state in strikes across Iran on Feb. 28, sparking the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Saudi Arabia, one of the world's richest nations and a key American ally, is now bearing the brunt of the Houthis' attacks, which have killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports over the last week. Along with other allied groups, the militants have also attacked Saudi oil infrastructure, helping drive up global energy prices by threatening the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which, like the Strait of Hormuz, is a key maritime chokepoint for oil and gas shipments.
The Saudis have asked the U.S. to join its military operations against the Houthis, and President Trump, who initially rejected the request, said over the weekend that he's considering it.
Iran's "most powerful proxy"
The Houthis are backed financially and militarily by Iran, officials from the U.S. and Israel, as well as many regional analysts, have said for years.

They were once a relatively marginal group within what Iran calls its Axis of Resistance — a loose alliance of anti-Israel, anti-U.S. militant groups that includes Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Both of those U.S.-designated terrorist organizations have been severely weakened by Israeli operations launched in the wake of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023.

The Houthis joined Hamas and Hezbollah's attacks on Israel and became the target of an Israeli counteroffensive, as well as military operations by the Biden and Trump administrations. But unlike Hamas and Hezbollah, the group has rebounded and emerged better armed, battle-hardened and confident.

"The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," said Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next."
After the 2023 attack on Israel, with help from Iran, the group really started gaining capacity and momentum.

"Before Oct. 7, we didn't see them getting the newest equipment from Iran. After Oct. 7, they got the best," al-Basha told CBS News, adding that Tehran not only armed the Houthis, but also helped the group hone its skills in penetrating air defenses.
The Houthis started adopting new tactics, including targeting Israel with layered attacks using drones, cruise missiles and then ballistic missiles to overwhelm the country's significant defenses.
Now the Houthis are using the same tactics against Saudi Arabia.

In the age of asymmetric warfare, the group has also used Yemen's ranking as one of the poorest countries in the world as something of a strategic advantage: They rely on a strongly ideological support base willing to suffer economic pain and isolation if the tradeoff is inflicting great damage to the Saudis and the global economy, said Yoel Guzansky, a senior research fellow focused on Persian Gulf politics and security at the Institute for National Security Studies.
"All you need is a not very sophisticated surface-to-surface missile to strike Riyadh airport. They can assemble those in small factories in the mountains," Guzansky said.
What do the Houthis want?
Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said recently that the group's attacks on Saudi Arabia are in response to a "brutal Saudi aggression against our country and our people."
But al-Basha said the Houthis' real objectives are not retaliation, but power and recognition.

They want to seize control of all of Yemen, and to get the Saudis to both recognize their legitimacy, and help bankroll their expansion, he said, which is why he believes they have coupled their campaign inside Yemen with the attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis' Iran-powered evolution

The Houthi movement grew out of the Zaydi Shiite Muslim sect, which has roots that date back centuries in northern Yemen. They are a minority in the country, which is predominantly Sunni Muslim, but the number of Zaydis is significant, representing as much as a third of Yemen's overall population.

The Houthi movement originally emerged as an effort to protect Zaydi culture within Yemen, but it evolved into a group that has as its slogan: "Allah is the Greatest; Death to America; Death to Israel; A Curse upon the Jews; Victory to Islam."
Analysts estimate that the armed Houthi force consists of hundreds of thousands of combat-ready fighters. The group itself claims to have trained more than a million militants.

Their march to real power began in 2012, when the then-much-smaller group, consisting of thousands of fighters, capitalized on unrest in Yemen following the Arab Spring ouster of longtime authoritarian President Ali Abdullah Saleh to build a loyal following in the north of the country.

In 2014, they seized the capital Sanaa, sparking a civil war with the Western- and Saudi-backed government. The government was forced to relocate to the southern port city of Aden, where it is still based, and it has also retained control of the less-populated eastern portion of the country.
The Houthis quickly took control of key state military and civilian powers, including missile brigades and special forces, and the ability to levy taxes, explained al-Basha.

The group survived a first round of fighting with the Saudi-led military coalition from 2015 until 2022. During that time, military advisers from Hezbollah and Iran helped train Houthi commanders and combatants — and built up the group's ability to manufacture its own weapons, including drones and missiles, according to analysts.

The Houthis may also be using AI software to fine-tune their weapons. U.S. tech firm Anthropic released a report in September saying it had identified "threat actors" based in northern Yemen using their Claude Code software "in place of human software engineers to develop the guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) software that steers and stabilizes a flying vehicle."

The weapons the unnamed actors were attempting to develop included guided rockets and multi-stage ballistic missiles, according to Anthropic, which said it did not have evidence of the actors successfully fielding an operational device.

While they can produce some of their own weapons, however, Fabian Hinz, a weapons analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies, wrote last year that the Houthis "remain dependent on Iran for key technologies and advanced capabilities. While Tehran's support has, in some areas, evolved from the direct provision of complete systems to enabling localized manufacturing, it remains a critical enabler of Houthi military activity."
But it is not a one-sided relationship.

"With Hamas and Hezbollah severely weakened, the Houthis have become an increasingly indispensable pillar of Iran's regional strategy, providing Tehran with a relatively resilient and cost-effective means of threatening Saudi Arabia, Israel, and international shipping while projecting power far beyond Yemen," Guzansky told CBS News. "Their strategic value to Iran has arguably never been greater, even if the Houthis retain considerable autonomy in their decision-making."
Yemen's devastating war

Situated at the southern end of the Arabian Peninsula, the Houthis are geographically isolated from any outside ground force, with the exception of the Saudis, who don't have the manpower to take on such a well-entrenched enemy, analysts say.

Domestically, in Yemen's vicious civil war, the well-coordinated group faces opposing forces that, while largely aligned with the Saudi-backed government, are themselves divided and operating under separate command structures.
Since Yemen descended into war in 2015,  the United Nations estimates that some 377,000 people have died, more than half due to indirect causes such as starvation and disease amid the fighting.
More than 201,210 people have fled from their homes, according to data from the United Nations' International Organization for Migration, including more than 3,700 who have fled by sea to Djibouti.

According to figures published by the World Health Organization last week, Yemen's Ministry of Health and Population had reported 959 deaths and 4,207 injuries attributed directly to the fighting across 10 provinces between the beginning of September and Oct. 2.
The Houthi-run Ministry of Health said Tuesday the death toll from the recent escalation of fighting, during the same period,  stood at 107, with 278 more wounded.

title: Pacific region sets record for big, long-lasting hurricanes
summary: The Pacific has broken a record for nasty, long-lasting hurricanes east of the international date line, turbocharged by the supersized El Niño​, scientists say.
story: The drumbeat of monster hurricanes in the Pacific has broken a record for nasty, long-lasting storms east of the international date line, turbocharged by nature's supersized El Niño, scientists said.

"Since September 20, when Odalys formed, it's been berserk," said Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach, who forecasts and studies storm activity. "This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful."

One of the key measurements meteorologists use to judge hurricane seasons is called accumulated cyclone energy, or ACE, which includes a storm's wind speed and longevity. On Sunday, a section of the Pacific east of the date line, which brews storms headed for Hawaii, Mexico and the U.S. West Coast, passed the old mark set in 2018. The area is still going strong with Hurricane Simon and appears on the verge of spawning another one that will really ramp up in strength, Klotzbach said.
On Tuesday, the Pacific will tie a record for most days with a hurricane spinning and is likely to break it soon after that, Klotzbach said.
"It feels like almost everything that can spin up does spin up," said University of Arizona atmospheric scientist Kim Wood.

Several meteorological factors have come together to supercharge the Pacific, chief among them the El Niño, Klotzbach and other hurricane researchers said. An El Niño weakens and shifts the high-altitude vertical winds that otherwise can dampen or even decapitate storms. In the Pacific, that wind shear runs east to west, generally with the direction storms travel, so it's like riding a bicycle with a tailwind, Klotzbach said.

Meanwhile, the weather pattern has dampened hurricanes in the Atlantic, where the ACE is less than 18% of what's normal for this time of year. El Niño makes the wind shear in the Atlantic like riding into a headwind, he said.
The Atlantic basin set a record this year for its longest stretch without any hurricanes developing. Isaias was its first, on Oct. 7.

Another factor is warm water, which serves as hurricane fuel. By definition, El Niño is a warming of the equatorial Pacific that changes weather worldwide. In the Pacific storm basin, it's several degrees Fahrenheit warmer than normal, said Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of storm atmospheric sciences at the University at Albany in New York.

Usually in the Pacific, the extra warm storm-friendly water doesn't run as deep as it does in the Atlantic. So when one storm goes over a patch of water, it brings up cold water and makes it hard for a subsequent storm in the same area to stay alive, Wood said. But not this year.

Hurricane Rachel, whose remnants swamped Las Vegas over the weekend, didn't suffer as it went over, churned up by Category 5 Hurricane Polo, Wood said. She said the waters are warm from both El Niño and climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas.

Another factor in recent storms was a counterclockwise atmospheric spin over Central America - called a gyre - that spits out seeds of stormy weather that can form into hurricanes. It spit out both the Atlantic's Isaias and the Pacific's Simon at about the same time, Corbosiero and Klotzbach said.

The last five Pacific hurricanes — long-lasting Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel and Simon — have all reached major status with winds of at least 111 mph. Nolo, Odalys and Simon hit Category 4, while Polo set the record for time spent at Category 5 at two-and-a-half days.
When Klotzbach made those calculations on the record-breaking activity of the eastern and central Pacific, he looked at all storms east of the date line.

That's a slightly different approach from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which breaks that broad area into two regions. Neither NOAA-defined region is quite at record levels for ACE yet but, put together, they are.
Part of that is because often when one of those subregions is more active, the other isn't quite as crazy, but in 2026 they both are hyperactive, Wood said.

"This is the first year that both sides have been this active together," Wood said. "Usually, it's kind of focused more on one or the other, so that speaks to just the wide extent across this region of where there's been that lower shear, those warmer waters, and that higher moisture."

Off the Mexican coast is a disturbance that the National Hurricane Center gives a 90% chance of becoming Tropical Storm Trudy, which then could power up to something big, Klotzbach and Corbosiero said.

"It seems like that area is just one after another. So I would not be surprised to have another storm," Corbosiero said. "This year, because of the El Niño, we do have very favorable conditions. So as long as there's some sort of the seeds either from the gyre or from remnant ends of cold fronts, it seems like this is going to continue for a bit."

title: Zelenskyy says Russia isn't honoring Trump's energy ceasefire
summary: Within a day of President Trump announcing an "energy ceasefire," Ukraine said Russia had struck a power plant and other energy facilities across the country.
story: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that so far, "there is no indication that Russia is complying" with an energy ceasefire announced by President Trump the day before.
Just hours after Mr. Trump's announcement, Zelenskyy said Russia struck a power plant in eastern Ukraine. By Monday afternoon, Russia had attacked six additional energy facilities across Ukraine.

"Ukraine is ready to guarantee the energy ceasefire, as announced by the American President, and Russia must take corresponding steps," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "As of now, there is no indication that Russia is complying with the conditions outlined by the American President."

Asked Monday about reports that Russia had violated the energy ceasefire, Mr. Trump said: "I'm not sure about that, and we'll take a look. But all I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war." He also said "there's been violations on both sides."
The U.S. president later told reporters that he believes Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy."
Over the last year, Mr. Trump has made several attempts at brokering deals to halt strikes on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine that failed to materialize or were quickly violated.

In January, Mr. Trump claimed that Putin agreed not to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure for a week, but Russia attacked Kyiv's power and heating plants four days later. In September, Mr. Trump said both Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to refrain from striking one another's energy infrastructure, but neither side halted attacks.
Zelenskyy told CBS News in an interview after the September proposal that Ukraine would be willing to agree to such a moratorium but doubted Russia would ever reciprocate.

One reason for the Kremlin's intransigence is that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have a relatively greater impact than Ukraine's. Ukrainian strikes primarily target Russian oil and gas infrastructure, attempting to cut into the energy revenues Russia uses to fund its war effort.

The attacks have brought Russian oil refining to a 20-year low and reduced diesel production by 30% in 2026, according to the International Energy Agency, but Russia's economy has shown little sign of collapse.

"For Russia, Ukraine's attacks are an inconvenience and an inflationary pressure," Alexander Kolyandr, director for Europe at Eurasia Group, told CBS News. "It is definitely damaging Russia's economy, but it isn't putting it on the verge of collapse."

Russia — with more drones and missiles and an economy 10 times the size of Ukraine's — is able to inflict more relative pain on both the country's economy and its civilians. Ukraine has already begun to experience power outages this fall as Russia hammers its power grid heading into winter.

"Because the Ukrainian economy is so much smaller than the Russian one, the relative effect is much higher," Kolyandr said. "And the Russians by and large do not distinguish between civilian and military infrastructure. Their theory is that any kind of infrastructure is used or can be used for military purposes."

Last winter, as Ukrainians faced frequent power and heating outages through one of the coldest winters in recent memory, Mr. Trump requested Putin stop striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. This week, though, he has directed pressure toward Ukraine.

The pressure comes as Mr. Trump grapples with high global energy prices — a situation he has argued has more to do with the Russia-Ukraine war than the Iran war. Last week, Mr. Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to sell some diesel to the U.S. and global markets, a change of course after years of U.S. efforts to block Russia from financing its war effort by selling petroleum products abroad.

A European official and a Ukrainian official told CBS News that the Trump administration has threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine does not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.

The Ukrainian official said that Ukraine's government is taking the threats very seriously as intelligence sharing allows Ukraine to know where and when Russia launches its ballistic missiles from, and the PURL program is the only way Ukraine can purchase its Patriot air defense missiles, already in short supply.
The Financial Times was first to report the American threats to pause intelligence and weapons shipments to Ukraine.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.
Zelenskyy said progress toward an energy ceasefire hinges on the White House's willingness to impose more pressure on Russia.
"A lot depends on America's position for de-escalation to actually succeed," he wrote on X. "Pressure on Russia is needed."

title: Hackers heat up refrigerators at hundreds of supermarkets
summary: The cyberattack caused refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, sparking fires and forcing spoiled food to be thrown away.
story: Major French supermarket chains on Monday said they were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, forcing spoiled food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.
Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarché and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they suffered a cyberattack that Cooperative U's chief executive described as "unprecedented."

"Food security requires more attention at all levels," said the EU's food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such "exploitation of food" was now a "reality."
At least 300 shops of Intermarché or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements.

"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher wrote on X.
Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had sparked fires.
BFM TV said hackers "managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores."
The affected branches will have to "throw away all of the products" that are fresh and frozen, Intermarché told AFP.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were attacked but that the vast majority of its 6,000 stores were not affected, according to the Reuters news agency.
E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP "that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," resulting in "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores."
A source close to the issue said refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment was "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates."

It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using "outdated firmware." It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures on how many systems were affected.

Dutch supermarket operator Ahold Delhaize, which also has operations in the United States, said it was also dealing with a "security issue" in its network, Reuters reported. A phone app for the retailer told clients that due to a "cybersecurity incident" it was unable to deliver groceries.
"Large-scale cyberattack"

A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France's cybersecurity agency had already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor."

"It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected," and is seeking "to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them" and "prevent the spread," the source added.

The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France."
The probe will help "identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires," the prosecutor's office said.
Intermarché condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures.
BFM TV said temperatures were "altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products."
Rising fears of hybrid attacks
The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by malicious actors carrying out cyberattacks.

President Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered measures to protect France's critical infrastructure from Russian "hybrid attacks."

Industrial equipment such as refrigeration units, long isolated from the internet, is now connected via sensors or remote monitoring systems, Antoine Hautin of cybersecurity consultancy Almond told AFP.
By likely affecting hundreds of units simultaneously, the attack demonstrated "a certain level of sophistication," he added.

title: Stolen Renoir paintings found hidden behind cinder block wall
summary: Thieves broke into the museum and escaped with two works by Renoir, abandoning two others as they fled. The value of all four paintings was estimated at $10 million.
story: Two paintings by impressionist master Pierre-Auguste Renoir, stolen from a museum in southern France and later discovered hidden behind a wall, have sustained slight damage, prosecutors said on Monday.
A 29-year-old man seen as the main suspect was charged over the weekend after DNA evidence linked him to the theft.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and escaped with two works by Renoir, abandoning two others as they fled.
The value of all four paintings had been estimated at $10 million.
On Friday, authorities announced that the two outstanding stolen works had been found.
They were a portrait titled "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano" and a depiction of a woman at a well called "Young Woman at the Well."
Speaking to reporters in Paris, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said the paintings were recovered last Thursday during a search of a home in the southern town of Clermont-l'Herault.
The discovery of the stolen works followed the arrest of six people, including a woman, last Wednesday, said Bessone.

"The paintings were hidden behind a solid cinder block wall. They were completely undetectable," Bessone said. "It was through interrogation work that investigators were able to get the receiver of the stolen goods to admit that he had indeed taken possession of the paintings."

The two paintings were "in relatively good condition," although "the two works showed signs of damage," Bessone said, speaking alongside the head of France's national judicial police, Christian Sainte.
The frame of "Young Woman at the Well" was slightly damaged, while "the canvas of 'Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano' had a tear," Bessone said.
The tear was located "on the dress" in the portrait, the prosecutor said, adding that both paintings "will require restoration work."
String of recent heists
Culture Minister Catherine Pegard praised "the efficiency and determination of all those who made this outcome possible."
"Their commitment made it possible to recover these works in record time," the culture ministry said.
A spate of heists at French museums — including at the Louvre — has highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets.
Crown jewels valued at around $100 million were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris last year.
The suspected thieves have been arrested and charged, but none of the jewels have been recovered except for a crown that was dropped as the group escaped.
Other French museums have been targeted in recent months. In July, burglars stole millions of dollars worth of jewelry from the museum of French luxury glassmaker Lalique.
In October 2025, a woman was arrested and charged over the theft of gold from the Natural History Museum in Paris.

The month before that, thieves snatched three porcelain works worth millions of dollars and classed as national treasures in a heist at the Adrien Dubouche National Museum in Limoges in central France.

title: Pope Leo to undergo surgery after nodular lesion found in lung, Vatican says
summary: The American pope has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active
story: Pope Leo XIV will undergo surgery this week after a nodular lesion was found in his lung, the Vatican said. Recovery is expected to take a week.
Leo, 71, said Sunday that doctors recently discovered the nodular lesion during medical checks. He said it was found in an early stage and was "circumscribed."

"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo said in remarks during his Sunday noon blessing. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."
A statement by Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni didn't say when the pope would be hospitalized but that it would be in the "first days" of the week.
The Vatican said Monday that the pontiff is maintaining his regular schedule for the day as he awaits the surgery, according to the Reuters news service.
He was expected to be treated at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which has a special apartment for the pope.

A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1 inch that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.

"Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.

"When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis," he said in an email.

The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he planned to go.

The American pope has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo. This, Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said, is "an important starting point for coping as well as possible with treatment, including surgery."

Di Maio said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage, "the aim … is curative," he added.
Depending on what is found, possible treatments can include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, Di Maio told Italy's private Sky TG24.

"When we talk about something being localized, that can also refer to the need to establish whether the disease is confined to that one site or whether scans show signs of disease elsewhere," he said, adding that he has not treated the pope and was speaking about the disease in general.

Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.

title: Ethan Hawke blasts Hollywood's 'greedy bastards,' predicts massive rebellion against powerful elites
summary: Ethan Hawke predicts massive rebellion in music and live theater against Hollywood's "greedy bastards" who he says control the entertainment industry.
story: Ethan Hawke celebrates Willie Nelson’s 90th birthday and tells Fox News Digital ‘a lot of people disagree, but a lot of people can agree about Willie Nelson’
Ethan Hawke isn't holding back when it comes to the powerful forces he believes are controlling the entertainment industry.

During a new interview with GQ, the Oscar-nominated actor took aim at wealthy power players, blasting "greedy bastards" who think they control every aspect of Hollywood and predicting a major rebellion against the industry.

"I believe in rebellion. And I think people are going to wake up and punch back and there’s going to be massive movements in music and massive movements in live theater and massive movements of people getting together," Hawke said.
FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA
Ethan Hawke spoke about the "greedy bastards" who believe they control Hollywood. (Getty Images)

"So don’t worry that the money and the greedy bastards that think they control everybody, they always lose in the end," he continued. "And they’re all going in the grave eventually. They think they’re winning, but they’re losing because their lives are worthless."
Hawke also expressed frustration with the financial pressures shaping Hollywood, arguing that the projects actors care about most often come with the smallest paychecks.
TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS
"There's a direct correlation. I find that the more you love a project, the less you get paid," he said. "If you want to beat the algorithm, it's very difficult to do that and be paid."
Hawke found fame at a young age. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)
This isn't the first time Hawke has spoken about the pitfalls of Hollywood.
ROBERT DOWNEY JR. SLAMS MODERN CELEBRITY CULTURE AS 'ABSOLUTE HORSES---'
Last year, the actor called celebrity a "poison" for a young actor's brain.
During an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience," Hawke got candid about his start in Hollywood as a young man and reflected on the psychological effect of becoming famous at a young age.

"I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's poison. It's poison for your brain," the actor said. "To be a professional actor at a young age, it's dangerous in extremely insidious ways that are very, very hard to perceive when it's happening," Hawke said.

Rogan compared the experience of becoming famous as a child to concrete. If concrete is made incorrectly, with the wrong amount of water or cement, that's it, he explained. Rogan added that once it dries there is no way to repair or fix it.
Ethan Hawke at the 2026 BAFTAs on Feb. 22. (Getty Images)
DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH

"That analogy works for all walks of life. Really. If you have something really traumatic happen in childhood, it's very hard to recover. It's a tremendous amount of work to recover. And I agree with you, like I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's a poison. It's a poison for your brain," Hawke said.
During his GQ interview, Hawke expressed the same sentiment.

"I wouldn’t be the first person to say that there’s an aspect of celebrity that is like a disease," he said. "And you can handle little bits of it, but too much of it — we can see what happened to Elvis and we can see Michael Jackson. It’s a form of isolation. It’s like being put in a zoo, and zoo animals go nuts. So do human beings."

"And it seems like a kind of nice isolation because people are giving you money, and they’re telling you you’re wonderful, but nobody’s being real with you," he continued. "And that makes people insane. And they start scratching, trying to find some real life. And sometimes people do that with drugs, some people do that with acting out or getting in fights or whatever the ways that people do it."
Hawke once referred to celebrity as a "poison." (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for BFI)
Last year, fellow actor Dakota Johnson also ripped into Hollywood, calling the industry an absolute "mess."

"I think it’s hard when creative decisions are made by a committee, and it’s hard when creative decisions are made by people who don’t even really watch movies or know anything about them … that tends to be what’s occurring a lot," Johnson shared with host Sean Evans.
Johnson, who has grown up in the business as the daughter of actors Melanie Griffith and Don Johnson, is no stranger to the inner workings of Hollywood.
The "Fifty Shades of Grey" actress’ comments come as studios continue to create sequels and remakes, with original storytelling often sidelined.
Actress Dakota Johnson called Hollywood an absolute "mess." (Photo by Christopher Polk/CBS via Getty Images)

"When something does well … studios want to keep that going so they remake the same things," she claimed. "But humans don’t want that. They want fresh. They want to feel new things, experience new things, see new things."

title: 'Jon & Kate Plus 8' star Collin Gosselin accuses mom of trying to 'bury' him to ‘protect her reputation’
summary: Collin Gosselin alleges Kate Gosselin tried to "bury" him to protect her reputation, detailing childhood abuse claims and demanding accountability.
story: ‘In the Shadow of Eight’ author tells Fox News Digital he's willing to hear from estranged mom Kate Gosselin but insists she must own up to her alleged treatment of him during childhood.

Collin Gosselin is taking aim at his estranged mother, Kate Gosselin, accusing the former reality TV star of trying to "bury" him to protect her public image as he makes allegations of childhood abuse in his new memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight."

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, the "Jon & Kate Plus 8" alum said he has not spoken to Kate since he was 13 and would need an apology and accountability before considering reconciliation.
"I'd like an apology, simply put, an apology and for her to admit, and just take accountability for what she did," Collin, 22, said.
COLLIN GOSSELIN SENDS CRYPTIC SIGNAL TO MOM KATE AFTER CLAIMS SHE'S 'SPIRALING' OVER HIS UPCOMING MEMOIR
Collin Gosselin claimed his mother, Kate Gosselin, had him institutionalized against his will. (Michael Simon)

In his memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of My Childhood," Collin alleged he endured physical abuse, isolation and forced psychiatric medication as a child. KATE GOSSELIN CALLED A 'MONSTER' IN SOCIAL MEDIA COMMENTS AFTER SON COLLIN ANNOUNCES MEMOIR

"It was heavy on my heart, my whole life, but especially now, it was just, I just felt like it was the time to do that," he said.
The rift with Kate remains deep. Collin recalled a visit from his mother when he was 13, claiming the encounter left him with a painful final memory.
"She berated me for all of 20 minutes after not seeing me for over a year," he said.
KATE GOSSELIN DEFENDS HERSELF AGAINST SON COLLIN AS HE PREPARES TO RELEASE SHOCKING NEW MEMOIR

Collin also described the effects of the psychiatric medication he said he was allegedly forced to take as a child, saying it left him feeling like a "zombie." In his memoir, he portrayed his childhood away from the cameras that made his family famous as deeply isolating.
Collin Gosselin accuses his estranged mother, Kate Gosselin, of physical abuse, isolation and forcing him to take psychiatric medication during his childhood. (Getty Images)

Despite the estrangement, Collin said he had not ruled out taking a call from Kate. But forgiveness, he stressed, would not automatically mean reconciliation.

title: Kelly Clarkson 'has put us in danger,' Brooklyn store owner claims as bird's price tag soars to $15M
summary: Adam Rubin claims Kelly Clarkson's viral dispute over a mechanical singing bird has led to threats and doxxing against his Brooklyn curiosity shop.
story: Jay Aldebert says Clarkson’s first step should have been to contact the store’s owner and try to resolve the issue privately. If the owner dismissed her concerns or was rude, he says, she could then consider using her social media platform.
Kelly Clarkson's public clash with a Brooklyn shop has left its owner concerned about more than a lost sale.

Adam Rubin, co-owner of Art of Play and a children’s author, spoke with Fox News Digital inside the Brooklyn store Tuesday morning, claiming the singer has put his business in danger after their viral dispute over a $15,000 mechanical singing bird.
The bird at the center of the controversy now has a staggering $15 million price tag.

Art of Play co-owner Adam Rubin poses with Molly, a mechanical singing and dancing bird that has become a fixture at the Brooklyn shop. (Fox News Digital)
"But I am afraid for the safety of our shop. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," Rubin told Fox News Digital.
Rubin claimed the backlash has extended beyond angry comments online, with people associated with the business allegedly facing threats and having their personal information exposed.
"We've got incredible support from our neighbors and fans over the past few days, and all of them have been attacked, threatened, doxed," he said.

Rubin also accused Clarkson of an "abuse of power," arguing that the singer's enormous platform has intensified the backlash against his small business.
Rubin argued that Clarkson's celebrity status carries a responsibility.
"You can't just try to squash somebody like a bug and expect everybody to give you a pass," he said.

Rubin also questioned why strangers would go to such lengths to attack a small business on behalf of a celebrity, expressing frustration that people who had never visited his store were joining the backlash.
The mechanical bird that sparked the dispute has also undergone a dramatic price change.
A photograph taken Tuesday by Fox News Digital shows a new sign beside Molly identifying the bird as a creation of artist Bliss Kolb, with an eye-popping price of $15 million.
Molly, a mechanical singing bird designed by Bliss Kolb, is displayed at Art of Play in Brooklyn alongside a $15 million price tag and a look at its intricate inner workings. (Fox News Digital)

The new figure is 1,000 times the original $15,000 price at the center of Clarkson's complaint.

Art of Play previously explained in a public statement that the original $15,000 figure referred to a nearly identical automaton available from artist Bliss Kolb, while Molly herself is permanently attached to the wall and serves as a fixture in the store's magic performances.

Rubin also addressed the dramatic price change during his conversation with Fox News Digital, pointing to the attention Molly has received since Clarkson's visit.

Rubin suggested Molly's sudden notoriety has made her one of the most recognizable mechanical birds in the world.
The new sign offers a striking contrast to the original $15,000 price tag that Clarkson cited in her complaint.

KELLY CLARKSON'S STORE CALLOUT SHOWS THE 'POWER' OF CELEBRITY STATEMENTS: EXPERT

title: Joe Manganiello's secret seven-year health battle that nearly killed him
summary: Joe Manganiello reveals Sofia Vergara made the life-saving call to remove his large intestine while he was unconscious during a secret health crisis.
story: ‘America’s Got Talent’ judge Heidi Klum tells Fox News Digital if she would ever set up Sofia Vergara on a date.
Joe Manganiello is opening up about the secret health battle that nearly "took his life" over seven years.
Manganiello sat down with "CBS Mornings" to discuss his health and his newly released memoir, "Bloodlines."
During his appearance, the actor told Gayle King he was offered the role as the main villain, Deathstroke, in Ben Affleck's canceled "Batman" movie.
He wrote in his memoir that, at the same time as the job offer, he was "dying." Manganiello received the call to appear in the movie in 2016.
Joe Manganiello had to have his entire large intestine removed to save his life in 2016. (Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

"I got the call about a month out of the hospital after I collapsed on another set," Manganiello told King. "After about a year of feeling these mystery symptoms, I went into the hospital for two months straight and, at the end of my stay, they wound up having to remove my entire large intestine to save my life.
JOE MANGANIELLO DENIES SOFIA VERGARA’S CLAIM MARRIAGE ENDED BECAUSE HE WANTED A BABY: ‘SIMPLY NOT TRUE’

"They had split me open. My entire large intestine had turned to pus, and it was about to explode," he continued. "They took it out, and the surgery left me with an ostomy bag. And in the wake of that, I lost 60 pounds in two weeks. I couldn't walk. My eye went cross-eyed. I lost my voice. I had five catheters."
"I went into the hospital for two months straight and, at the end of my stay, they wound up having to remove my entire large intestine to save my life."
Manganiello explained that, after he was released from the hospital, he was in the process of trying to gain the weight back when he got the call to meet Affleck and appear in the "Batman" movie.
The actor told King he was still married to Sofia Vergara at the time, and she was the one who ultimately made the decision for the doctors to save his life and remove his large intestine.
Sofia Vergara and Joe Manganiello were married from 2015-2023. (WireImage)

"They had to call her as my next of kin and give her options of what she thought I would want done to me while I was unconscious. She chose the right one, and it bought me time," Manganiello said. "It didn't solve the problem. The doctors still had no idea what was causing this, how to treat it. But it bought me enough time."
"But we do have to credit her for saving your life. For making that decision," King replied.
"Absolutely," Manganiello said.

Joe Manganiello's "mystery illness" symptoms began shortly after he married Sofía Vergara. (FilmMagic)

title: Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after losing home of 46 years then his longtime friend Rob Reiner
summary: Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after losing his Pacific Palisades home in the wildfires and the death of close friend Rob Reiner.
story: Legal expert Donna Rotunno analyzes Nick Reiner's probable cause hearing in the murder case of his parents, Rob and Michele Reiner, and explains the low legal standard required to advance the case to trial. Rotunno also discusses the defense's strategy to dismiss charges against the man accused of fatally mowing down NHL star Johnny Gaudreau and his brother, a complex issue involving blood plasma vs. whole blood testing.
Billy Crystal is opening up about how a devastating year changed his relationship with God.

During an interview with CBS Sunday Morning, the comedian, 78, opened up about how losing his longtime Pacific Palisades home in the January 2025 wildfires and the death of his close friend Rob Reiner greatly impacted his faith.

Crystal was asked whether he had been speaking with God after the painful losses. The actor referenced his previous one-man show, "700 Sundays," in which he described conversations with God, before offering a stark response.
BILLY CRYSTAL DESCRIBES PAIN OF LOSING HOME IN PALISADES FIRE AT FIREAID BENEFIT CONCERT: ‘FELL TO MY KNEES’
Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after a year of loss.  (Getty Images for Peabody Awards)
"No, ’cause I don’t trust Him," Crystal said.
"Too many bad things have happened," he added. "The Earth is in bad shape. This is a weird, scary time. So no, not anymore."

Crystal’s longtime home was destroyed in the Palisades fire after he and his wife, Janice, lived there for 46 years. The couple raised their children and grandchildren in the house, which Crystal described as a "magical place."
Speaking at a benefit weeks after the disaster, Crystal recalled visiting the remains of what was once his home.
ERIKA KIRK PENS ESSAY ON GRIEF AS READERS GAIN INSIGHTS INTO WRENCHING PAST YEAR

"When we were finally able to get back to our house in the Palisades, which I lived in for 46 years, like thousands of you, our house now looked like this," Crystal said, before a photo of the aftermath of the Palisades Fire appeared on the screen.
Billy Crystal lost his home of 46 years in the Pacific Palisades fire in 2025.  (Getty Images)

"I stepped onto the grounds and fell to my knees and I wailed. I had not cried like that since I was 15 years old, and I was told that my father had just died. I remember looking in the mirror back then with my whole life ahead of me thinking, ‘What’s my life gonna be like without him?'"
"And now folks, I'm 76-years-old, without a mirror and a lot less life to ponder thinking, ‘What is my life going to be like without our home?’" Crystal asked.

The loss became the inspiration for Crystal’s new Broadway show, "860," which is named after the street address of the home. The production recreates his home office onstage and explores his family, career, memories and grief.
NICK REINER INDICTED IN MURDERS OF PARENTS ROB REINER, MICHELE SINGER REINER AT BRENTWOOD HOME
"860" also reflects on the loss of Reiner, who was killed with his wife, Michele, in December 2025. Crystal said he and Reiner had been together at a holiday party the night before their deaths.
Crystal, pictured with the late Rob Reiner and Meg Ryan, says Reiner's death affected him in more ways than one.  (Gregg DeGuire/FilmMagic)
"We said goodbye," Crystal recalled. "And then … what?!?"
Despite the tragedies, Crystal said humor has helped him move forward.
"That’s what I do," he said when asked how he finds humor during the darkest moments. "It’s a healer."
Crystal said performing "860" has already helped him process the loss of his home and friends.

"I’ve absorbed the biggest pains that people couldn’t go through — the loss of home, dearest of friends," he said. "And I’m OK."

title: 'Moonshiners' stars challenge notorious warning that outlaw liquor can make you go blind
summary: Mark Ramsey and Digger Manes from "Moonshiners" challenge stereotypes about Appalachia's distillers as home distilling battles reach the Supreme Court.
story: Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes of "Moonshiners" discuss the history of Appalachian moonshining, its misunderstood reputation and why they believe the tradition will survive.
Moonshine’s reputation is enough to make your eyes water.

For generations, Americans have been warned that the notorious outlaw liquor could leave them blind. But "Moonshiners" stars Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes say there's more behind that warning than most people realize.
"There's a huge different thought process behind moonshine than there was, say, in the '40s, '30s, early years," Manes told Fox News Digital.
KENNY LAW, 'MOONSHINERS' STAR, DEAD AT 68
Mark Ramsey and his distilling partner Digger Manes are starring in the new season of Discovery Channel's "Moonshiners," which airs on Tuesdays at 8 p.m. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"There was a lot of propaganda out there. It was said that it could make you go blind, make you die, make you go crazy, make you get the jack leg. The government was the one that was poisoning the industrial alcohol the people were stealing to make bathtub gin."

Historical records support part of Manes' account. During Prohibition, the federal government required industrial alcohol to contain toxic additives to discourage people from drinking it, according to the Smithsonian Channel. Some of that alcohol was diverted into the illegal liquor market and sold for consumption, although it was distinct from traditionally distilled moonshine.
Mark Ramsey learned about producing moonshine as a young man. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

The consequences were deadly. According to the Smithsonian Channel, 66 people died in New York City on Christmas Day 1926 after consuming poisoned industrial alcohol. The city's medical examiner, Charles Norris, blamed the federal government's practice of adding toxic substances to industrial alcohol, including those involving methyl alcohol, also known as methanol, which can cause blindness and death.
WATCH: ‘MOONSHINERS’ STARS REVEAL THE TRUTH BEHIND A MISUNDERSTOOD TRADITION
But not every warning about illicit liquor was a scare tactic.
Ramsey acknowledged that moonshine posed genuine health risks in earlier generations, particularly when distillers unknowingly used dangerous materials to build their equipment.
Eric "Digger" Manes (pictured here) and Mark Ramsey have mastered the craft of distillation. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"Back in the day, there were people who had health issues because of moonshine," Ramsey explained. "The solder that they used to build the pots had lead in it back in the day, and they didn't know that it was happening. So once it was discovered that the solder had lead in it, even the old timers here, when they built their stills, they no longer soldered their joints on the inside of the pots. All the solder connections were on the outside where the mash never touched the solder anymore."

A moonshine still recently confiscated by the Internal Revenue Bureau is photographed at the Treasury Department between 1921 and 1932. A man stands next to the still and looks at the contents of a glass. (Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
"So yeah, it caused some issues, but it was strictly an accident," he said. "They just didn’t know any better."

While moonshine does not inherently cause blindness, improperly produced spirits can contain dangerous levels of methanol, a toxic form of alcohol. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that methanol poisoning can damage the optic nerve, causing permanent vision loss or death.
According to Discovery.com, "A dozen surviving moonshiners must join forces to fight for their way of life, before it's gone forever." (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"Moonshiners," which is now in its 16th season, premiered in 2011. The series follows "a diverse group of people living in Appalachia who carry on a 200-year-old tradition passed down from their forefathers, making moonshine," according to the show's synopsis.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Discovery Channel's "Moonshiners" has been airing since 2011. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

Distillers can legally produce and sell spirits marketed as moonshine if they comply with federal, state and local licensing, taxation and other requirements. Federal law generally prohibits producing distilled spirits at home for personal consumption, according to the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, although recent court rulings have challenged the constitutionality of certain restrictions.
According to The Washington Post, federal appeals courts have issued conflicting rulings on a federal restriction on home distilling dating back to 1868.
Mark Ramsey, Amanda Bryant, Kelly Williamson and Eric "Digger" Manes are seen here during the filming of "Moonshiners." (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

In April 2026, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a federal restriction prohibiting distilled spirits plants from operating in homes and certain other locations was unconstitutional. Days later, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reached the opposite conclusion, upholding the restriction as a "necessary and proper means" of collecting liquor taxes, the outlet reported.
Barrels of moonshine age at Casey Jones Distillery in Hopkinsville, Kentucky., on Aug. 16, 2017. (Getty Images)

The Hobby Distillers Association and four individual plaintiffs challenged the restriction in the 5th Circuit case, according to The Washington Post. Supporters of legal home distilling hope overturning the restriction could spark a "craft spirits revolution."

The legal battle has since reached the Supreme Court. In July, John Ream, the plaintiff in the 6th Circuit case, asked the justices to review the ruling. The Justice Department filed a separate petition in August, seeking to overturn the 5th Circuit's decision.
Eric "Digger" Manes and Mark Ramsey are the faces of Sugarlands Distilling Company. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)
Ramsey also challenged longstanding stereotypes about "moonshiners."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Seth Powers, a production staffer at Maine Craft Distilling, boxes bottles of blueberry moonshine. The company is one of several distilleries and breweries to use Maine farm products. (Portland Press Herald via Getty Images)

"A lot of times, people give it a bad name because they just see it as poison and a bunch of heathens out doing stuff they shouldn’t do," he said. "And moonshiners, as a rule, are very, very good people. They were just simply doing what they had to do to survive back in the day."

"[Moonshine] didn't actually sell in Appalachia," Ramsey said. "It went farther north: Ohio, Detroit, New York, the East Coast. ... One of my friends told me ... he took a load of liquor to Ohio and said, 'Them fellas up there, they get it. And every one of them said, 'God bless them hillbillies.'"
Ole Smoky Tennessee Moonshine is seen here on Dec. 10, 2013, at The Garage by Kenneth Cole in New York City. (Getty Images)

"The liquor business back in the day, the heyday of it, probably wouldn't have flourished here in Appalachia so prominently had it not been for our northern neighbors buying it," Ramsey said. "So we had a reason to make it, and they had a reason to want it."
The launch of Original Moonshine at Morrison Hotel Gallery in New York City is seen here on Sept. 11, 2010. (Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
"We were broke, but could make liquor," Manes added. "And they had money and could buy it."
Ramsey is also optimistic about the future of moonshine. He said a new generation of distillers is eager to carry on the tradition.
Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes told Fox News Digital that moonshine became increasingly popular up north. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"As we saw in previous seasons … we always want to know who's going to fill our shoes, who's going to carry the torch forward," he said. "[And] we have so many good distillers up and coming. I think it's got a future, a very healthy one. Things will change. It's been argued that the best drink of liquor hasn't been made yet, so they've got something to shoot for."

Hall of Fame driver Junior Johnson's legal moonshine, Midnight Moon, was available at the bar during NASCAR's Fan Appreciation Day at the NASCAR Hall of Fame on Jan. 31, 2015, in Charlotte, N.C. (NASCAR via Getty Images)

"That's the most beautiful thing about the lessons you learn from these old timers that taught you how to make liquor," Manes said. "You make do with what you've got, and you don't let the situation you're standing in drag you down. You keep going forward."
For Manes, preserving the tradition comes down to pride in his craft.
Eric "Digger" Manes and Mark Ramsey are hopeful young people will want to learn the craft of producing quality moonshine. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"To me, it's more the pride," he said. "It's no different. I don't know what hobby you may have. It may be painting. You may paint pictures. Well, if you do a beautiful portrait, and you stand back, and you look at it, you think, 'Wow, that really does look good.'"

Ole Smoky Tennessee Moonshine is on display at Meatopia X: The Carnivore's Ball during the Food Network New York City Wine & Food Festival at Esurance Rooftop Pier 92 in New York City on Oct. 19, 2014. (John Parra/Getty Images)
Manes said he gets that same satisfaction from turning simple ingredients into moonshine.
"We take what other people would consider slop — that’s the conglomeration of cornmeal and sugar — and make a crystal-clear product that tastes good," he said. "And we love it."
Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes are seen here cleaning the inside of a still. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)
"Good thing about this business is it [doesn't] really have bad times," Ramsey said.

Moonshine runs from the still at Casey Jones Distillery in Hopkinsville, Kentucky., on Aug. 16, 2017. (Getty Images)
"If you’re down in the dumps, you drink to drown your sorrows," he joked. "If you’re happy, you drink to celebrate. So it’s got a good source of customers all the time."

title: White House official defends Teresa Giudice’s visit as critics slam reality star’s ex-husband’s pardon push
summary: Lynne Patton shared her cocaine addiction story and the intervention by Eric Trump and Lara Trump that shaped her belief in second chances for Joe Giudice.
story: The "Real Housewives of New Jersey" star told Fox News Digital that even though she and Joe Giudice are divorced she believes he belongs in the United States. Joe was deported in 2019 after serving 41 months in federal prison for fraud charges.

A senior White House official with longstanding ties to "The Real Housewives of New Jersey" star Teresa Giudice is addressing whether her ex-husband, Joe Giudice, deserves a second chance, while emphasizing that any presidential pardon decision rests solely with President Donald Trump.

Lynne Patton, deputy assistant to the president for coalition policy and engagement, took to Instagram to explain why Teresa Giudice and her daughter, Gia Giudice, were invited to the White House for Columbus Day and Italian American heritage celebrations.
Patton's comments about Joe, who was deported to Italy after serving time for fraud-related offenses, also addressed the family's efforts to secure a presidential pardon.
‘RHONJ’ ALUM JOE GIUDICE SAYS HE SHOULDN’T HAVE BEEN DEPORTED AFTER FRAUD CONVICTION
Teresa Giudice and her then-husband Joe Giudice walk on June 21, 2013, in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. The two finalized their divorce in September 2020. (Larry Marano/Getty Images)
Patton emphasized that she has no authority over presidential pardons but offered a personal message about redemption and second chances.

"For those inquiring @teresagiudice and her daughter, @_giagiudice, were at the White House at the invitation of the President & First Lady in honor of Columbus Day & Italian-American heritage. I have known Teresa and her family, including @joe.giudice, for nearly two decades," Patton began her post.
Lynne Patton, pictured here with President Donald Trump, has longstanding ties to the Giudice family. (My View with Lara Trump/Screengrab)

"I’ve attended family gatherings at their former New Jersey homes where Joe taught me how to roll meatballs & Teresa’s beloved father once showed me how to make his famous homemade wine. I am not in charge of pardons. Nor do I decide who receives them."
She added, "That is the President’s sole decision based upon recommendations from the White House Pardon Czar, @alicemariefree, and White House Counsel."
Teresa and Gia Giudice posing for a mirror selfie with Lynne Patton during the "Real Housewives" stars' visit to the White House. (Lynne Patton/Instagram)
Patton then shared her own experience with addiction and the second chance she said the Trump family gave her.
Patton said she relapsed into cocaine addiction while working at the Trump Organization in 2013, crediting Eric Trump and Lara Trump with staging an intervention that she said saved her life.
Her experience, she said, shaped her belief in second chances.

"In 2013 while working at the Trump Organization, I relapsed with cocaine addiction. @erictrump and his then girlfriend, @laraleatrump, held an emotional intervention for me that I credit with saving my life," Patton wrote on Instagram. (Lynne Patton/Instagram)

"To date, I have been drug-free for 13 years. They could have fired me. But instead, they told me that I was worth saving. Even when I didn’t believe that myself. Instead of sidelining me, they gave me more responsibility. I worked harder. Stayed in the office longer. Arrived earlier. More importantly, I earned back their trust & friendship. In turn, that translated into more self-confidence and earned promotions — including a personal request from their father to join him in D.C. It rebuilt my determination to succeed & help others do the same."
Patton also cited her Christian faith and the importance of a father's presence in his children's lives.
TODD AND JULIE CHRISLEY HOME FOR HOLIDAYS AFTER TRUMP PARDONS END PRISON TIME

"With that said, my faith in God compels me to believe that a father’s place is in the home. Statistics confirm the same. More importantly, so does the Bible. Charlie Kirk often declared that the biblical role of the father to his child is to be their protector, both physically and spiritually. Quality time is everything. And no, it is never too late to be the provider who God intended every father to be," Patton added.

"Do I believe that Joe deserves a second chance? Unfortunately, it is not my place to decide. But what I do know is that one of his beautiful daughters desperately needs him now more than ever. And even God supports that."
Joe was deported to Italy in 2019 after serving 41 months in federal prison for financial crimes. He has been living in the Bahamas, while his four daughters remain in the United States.
Teresa Giudice, Gia Giudice and Joe Giudice in 2014. ( Dave Kotinsky/Getty Images)

Gia has publicly advocated for her father's return to the United States. Joe sought a presidential pardon in June 2025, and Gia said in August 2026 that the family had filed a humanitarian packet as part of its efforts to bring him home.

A presidential pardon would not automatically guarantee Joe's return to the United States. According to the Justice Department, a pardon can eliminate certain grounds for deportation, but its immigration consequences depend on the circumstances of the case.

Members of the Giudice family commented on Patton's post, with Joe writing, "Your [sic] the best ❤️❤️❤️❤️."
Gia wrote, "thank you Lynn♥️🙏🏼," while her sister Milania commented, "thank you so much ❤️."
Teresa wrote, "We go way back ❤️," adding, "Love you ❤️."
However, Patton's remarks drew mixed reactions from Instagram users.
One Instagram user wrote, "What a beautiful post! That man did his time! Let him come home to his beautiful daughters!! Where he belongs!!!"
"I hope Joe is able to come back! They allow all these illegals here with no consequences, and most of them are repeat offenders and dangerous. Bring @joe.giudice home to his family," wrote another.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Teresa and ex-husband Joe Giudice pleaded guilty to fraud and each served time in prison. (Mike Coppola)
Another wrote, "He is a convicted felon who could have legalized citizenship years ago. Sorry but this nepotism and bravolebrity entitlement does not put him above the law."
"Explain how you pardon someone who isn’t a citizen. I care more about the affordability crisis than I do Bravo and Joe Guidice," another Instagram user said.

Patton's Instagram post included photos documenting her ties to the Giudice family and the Trump administration. One image showed Patton posing for a mirror selfie at what appeared to be the White House. Another showed Teresa and Gia seated on an ornate blue-and-gold sofa inside a formal White House room.

title: Selma Blair accused of kicking nurse hours after JFK plane arrest
summary: Selma Blair allegedly kicked a nurse in the chest at a Queens hospital hours after her arrest for an incident aboard a Delta flight to JFK Airport.
story: Actress Selma Blair appeared in Queens court after being accused of assaulting flight attendants, a police officer and a nurse following a Delta flight from Los Angeles to New York.

Selma Blair's alleged airline assault did not end with the police. She is also accused of kicking a nurse in the chest at a Queens hospital hours after she was arrested following an alleged in-flight incident aboard a Delta flight from Los Angeles to New York.

The criminal court affidavit, filed in Queens Criminal Court, says registered nurse Ashley DeLeo was assisting in transporting Blair for further medical treatment at Jamaica Hospital Medical Center at approximately 2 a.m. ET on Oct. 12 when Blair allegedly kicked her.
"The defendant kicked complainant DeLeo in her chest," the affidavit stated, adding that the alleged conduct caused "substantial pain to her chest."
SELMA BLAIR ARRESTED AFTER IN-FLIGHT INCIDENT

Selma Blair appears in Queens Criminal Court Monday, October, 12, 2026 in Queens, New York. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Barry Williams/ New York Daily News via Pool)

Blair, 54, was arraigned Monday on two counts of second-degree assault after Port Authority police responded to a call about a "physically abusive passenger" aboard Delta Flight 938, which had arrived at John F. Kennedy International Airport from Los Angeles, officials said.

The "Cruel Intentions" and "Hellboy" actress was taken into custody at JFK and transported to a hospital for evaluation. Two flight attendants reported injuries, and one was taken to a hospital, according to officials.
FRONTIER PASSENGERS TACKLE MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY CHOKED OFF-DUTY FLIGHT ATTENDANT, TRIED TO OPEN DOOR MID-FLIGHT
The court document also alleges Blair kicked a Port Authority police officer while being moved from JFK Terminal 4 into an ambulance at the airport’s B22 exit ramp.

Police Officer Maria Suarez was helping secure Blair on a stretcher at approximately 11:50 p.m. ET when Blair allegedly "removed her leg from the stretcher straps and kicked Officer Suarez repeatedly about the face, neck and chest," according to the affidavit.
CHAOS ERUPTS ON AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT AS UNRULY PASSENGER ALLEGEDLY BITES FELLOW TRAVELER MIDAIR
The affidavit says Suarez suffered swelling to her jaw and "substantial pain to her face, neck and chest." Suarez was treated at a local Queens-area hospital, according to the filing.
Delta said in a statement Monday that it has "zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first."

A representative for Blair said the actress suffered a medical emergency during the flight.
"Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct," Blair’s representative said. "Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition."
SEVERE TURBULENCE DIVERTS NEW YORK CITY FLIGHT TO MIAMI, 8 INJURED

Selma Blair exits Queens Criminal Court, Monday, October 12, 2026. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News)
Blair’s attorney said in court that the incident was not intentional and argued that she had missed doses of a "powerful" medication used to control severe neurological symptoms.
"This was not an intentional assault," attorney Shawn Barnes said.
Barnes also said Blair had been working "extensive hours" before the flight and claimed she fell and hit her head during the trip.
"These factors, coupled with altitude, resulted in a state of severe confusion and disorientation," Barnes said.
SELMA BLAIR SAYS 'NO ONE RETURNED MY CALLS' AFTER ANTI-ISLAM COMMENT LED TO HOLLYWOOD FALLOUT

Selma Blair appears in Queens Criminal Court on Monday, October, 12, 2026, in Queens, New York. The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Barry Williams/ New York Daily News via Pool)

title: Sean 'Diddy' Combs hospitalized with head injury while behind bars: report
summary: Sean "Diddy" Combs was reportedly rushed from FCI Fort Dix to a hospital for a head injury, though his team says they are working to confirm details.
story: Criminal defense attorney Donna Rotunno and former inmate Larry Levine join 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss the sentencing of music mogul Sean 'Diddy' Combs and what to expect from his time in prison.
Sean "Diddy" Combs was allegedly rushed from prison with a medical emergency, TMZ reported.
The outlet indicated Diddy, 56, was transported to a nearby hospital to treat a head injury. It remains unclear how the disgraced music mogul was injured.
Despite the reports circulating, Diddy's team and the Federal Bureau of Prisons could not confirm the alleged injuries.
INSIDE DIDDY'S PRISON LIFE WITH MASSAGES, BOOZE AND NUDE PHOTOS: REPORT
Sean "Diddy" Combs was reportedly hospitalized following a medical emergency. (Getty Images)
"We are aware of the reports concerning Sean Combs and are working to confirm the circumstances," reps confirmed to Fox News Digital.
"Sean’s health and well-being are our immediate concern, and we appreciate everyone who has reached out."
The Federal Bureau of Prisons could not provide a comment on Diddy's health or whereabouts.

"For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or medical status," the bureau said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.
DIDDY'S FEDERAL PRISON RELEASE DELAYED WEEKS AFTER REPORTED SOLITARY CONFINEMENT STINT
Sources told the outlet that Diddy remained conscious and speaking on his own while recovering from the alleged non-life-threatening injury.
Diddy was arrested and charged with multiple counts in September 2024. (Shareif Ziyadat)
Amid alleged medical woes, Diddy's prison release date has changed multiple times since he began serving his sentence.
According to multiple reports, the disgraced rap mogul was reportedly sent to solitary confinement in July after a prison fight with another inmate.
The incident began after a fellow inmate "made a remark to Combs, which instigated the event" at FCI Fort Dix, ABC News reported at the time.
CASSIE VENTURA FLED THE UNITED STATES AFTER TESTIFYING AGAINST DIDDY IN SEX CRIMES TRIAL: DOCS
Diddy was arrested in September 2024 on federal sex trafficking charges. (John Shearer/Getty Images)

Diddy was then reportedly sent to solitary confinement, the outlet noted. It's unclear if his release date was delayed due to the reported fight. He's now expected to be released from prison in March 2028.

In September 2024, the "Last Night" singer was arrested on federal sex trafficking charges after months of sexual misconduct allegations, lawsuits, investigations and the release of surveillance video that appeared to show the rapper severely beating then-girlfriend Cassie in the hallway of a Los Angeles hotel.
He was sentenced to more than four years behind bars in October after being convicted in July on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution.

Diddy was charged with racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking by force, fraud or coercion, and transportation to engage in prostitution in the indictment unsealed in September. (Jordan Strauss)

Diddy initially faced a maximum of life in prison if convicted on charges that included racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking by force, fraud or coercion, and transportation to engage in prostitution.

A jury convicted Diddy on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution on July 2, 2025. The "I'll Be Missing You" rapper was acquitted of the most serious charges of racketeering and sex trafficking.

title: Sylvester Stallone calls himself an 'idiot' for doing his own stunts, details nine back surgeries
summary: Sylvester Stallone reveals nine back surgeries and three neck fusions from doing his own stunts, calling himself an "idiot" for the decades of damage.
story: Stallone reflects on the toll of decades in action movies, citing nine back operations, three neck fusions and other injuries. He says performers should leave stunts to the professionals.
Sylvester Stallone admitted that he was an "idiot" for performing his own stunts after extensive medical procedures.
During an interview with Fox News Digital, the "Tulsa King" star opened up about the "millions" of regrets he has after decades of being an action star.

"Millions, millions of regrets. I could literally spend a half hour talking about injuries, the amount, not even like one, I'm talking about 30 hours, 30 minutes of just individual ones, because it becomes compounded. I have been injured many, many times, but after 'Expendables,' I ended up with nine back operations, three neck fusions. Both shoulders ripped out, eye, you know, all kinds of lens put ... it's been brutal," Stallone began.
Sylvester Stallone called himself an "idiot" for performing his own stunts. (2026 NBCUniversal Media, LLC)
Stallone admitted that he's never been "quite the same" since the surgeries.
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE
"Now you have to like make peace with the pain as much as you can," he shared.
WATCH: Sylvester Stallone calls himself an 'idiot' for doing his own stunts
The biggest lesson he has now, at 80 after decades of crazy stunt work, is to "let other people do their job."
"I think I'm an idiot for doing that."

"Don't be a stage hawk, or whatever you call it, a showboat. I know a lot of people are thinking about doing stunts ... don't. Don't. Let the pro do it," Stallone said. "Let me explain something, you cannot beat gravity, when you hit the ground, you lose, and it's going to come back."

He continued, "I mean, just ask every football player in the world. So yeah, that and people go, 'Aren't you proud of them?' No. I think I'm an idiot for doing that. I'm proud that I broke myself in pieces. Like, duh, no."
The Stallone-led "Tulsa King" is gearing up to release its fourth season on Oct. 16. The actor told Fox News Digital what still excites him about his character, Dwight Manfredi.

"He still hasn't achieved his goal, just when he thinks he's arrived, another situation, another dramatic episode presents itself, which is exactly what the show needs. We don't want him to be like, 'I can finally exhale.' No, you don't wanna," Stallone said.
Sylvester Stallone and Dolph Lundgren starred in "The Expendables" franchise. (Kiyoshi Ota/Getty Images)

Stallone said the new season opens with a jolt, putting Dwight under pressure from new enemies and tensions within his own crew.

"Well, it's quite shocking to start off with because certain elements happen that it's ... quite unnerving. And now I'm presented with a new level of, you might say, adversaries, gangsters, criminals that are coming at me technologically, politically, and mafioso-ishly from New York," he said. "So, I'm getting bombarded from all sides. Plus, I have internal struggles with some of my own crew. So it's kind of like having like a cuckoo's nest and trying to reign it all in, you know what I mean?"
"Tulsa King" season 4 comes out on Friday, October 16, 2026, on Paramount+.
Sylvester Stallone and Jennifer Flavin currently live in Florida. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)
Stallone also discussed a major change in his life outside of Hollywood: moving from California to Florida.

He told Fox News Digital the move helped him feel "invigorated" after he began growing complacent in California.

"In New York, I was a New York animal, like we all are here, I just said, you have to be. And then I got to California and I thought I was in Nirvana," Stallone began. "I did very well in California. And then California sort of changed. And became more populous and everything else. And I felt myself becoming very complacent and dull."
Stallone and his wife, Jennifer Flavin, moved out of California for Florida permanently in 2024.

"When we went to Florida, I didn't know one person. And now we have a great circle. So it's the best move. And my wife was also ... I think a lot of people would like to get a little peace and quiet. You know, they've been around so many billions of people that actually have water and birds and things like that. There's something that's invigorating and nourishing, and I think goes to our biology that makes us happier," he said.
Sylvester Stallone as Dwight Manfredi in "Tulsa King" Season 4. (Steve Swisher/Paramount+)

Flavin and Stallone share three daughters: Sophia, Sistine and Scarlet. His oldest daughter, Sophia, announced her engagement to boyfriend Michael Sheehan in August.
Stallone told Fox News Digital that Sheehan is making him "look bad."
WATCH: Sylvester Stallone says Dwight Manfredi still hasn’t achieved his goal

"I thought I actually did it pretty well because she found a guy that I wish every woman found. So I went, 'Wow, he's making me look bad.' With the flowers and this and the constant, 'Oh, here's breakfast, honey.' I went wow, calm down, guys, you're gonna make it terrible for us," Stallone said. "But he is very nurturing. So I actually wish I was sort of like that when I was younger. I didn't learn those skills from my family. A good morning was good morning, punch in the face. He's wonderful and two more to go."
